As illustrated in Fig. 4(c), each single spinon is equivalent to a bound state of two anti-spinons of the other two colors. These pairs can each be split at energy cost 2​J2​a2J_{2a}. For the spinon located at +𝒙^+\hat{\bm{x}}, we move the resulting anti-spinons along +𝒚^+\hat{\bm{y}} and +𝒛^+\hat{\bm{z}}, and similarly for the other two spinons. This results in an anti-spinon pair—equivalent to a single spinon each—located at the three octahedra at 𝒙^+𝒚^\hat{\bm{x}}+\hat{\bm{y}}, 𝒙^+𝒛^\hat{\bm{x}}+\hat{\bm{z}}, and 𝒚^+𝒛^\hat{\bm{y}}+\hat{\bm{z}}. These three spinons can then to the octahedron at 𝒙^+𝒚^+𝒛^\hat{\bm{x}}+\hat{\bm{y}}+\hat{\bm{z}} and mutually annihilate to return to the vacuum. This process results in the minimal vacuum-to-vacuum spin flip, or “fluctuator” [31, 32], involving twelve spins arranged on the edges of a cube as shown in Fig. 6(a); arrows indicate the relative directions the spins must point for this cluster to be flippable at zero energy cost. Note that as a process of flipping single spins, this vacuum-to-vacuum fluctuation requires passing through intermediate states with at least four spinons, with total energy cost 4×2​J2​a4\times 2J_{2a}.

We refer to this structure as a “cage”. Larger vacuum-to-vacuum fluctuators can be formed by such spinon proliferation and recombination processes, and we refer to these in general as “cage moves”, by analogy with the “loop moves” of spin ice [81, 82, 115]. In particular, one can combine many copies of the minimal cube to form large contractible flippable cages. General cages can be built from straight oriented segments representing lineon trajectories, which are glued together at corners where three lineons are created or annihilated. This includes, as a special case, a single straight line, meaning that fully polarized chains can be flipped at zero energy cost. For a system with periodic boundaries, this corresponds to creating a spinon/anti-spinon pair, sending one of them around a non-contractible handle of the torus, then re-annihilating the pair. Figure 6(b) illustrates a cage which includes a non-contractible winding. These structures correspond precisely to the generalized Wilson loops of fracton gauge theories [137]. Thus, they give rise to a fracton CSL—a classical cage-net condensate [83].

V.2 Thermodynamics from Cluster Monte Carlo Simulations

Having established the vacuum-to-vacuum “tunneling” processes characterizing this putative CSL, it remains to demonstrate the thermodynamic stability of the underlying Ising model against the development of any ordering instabilities. This means that the system possesses a non-zero ground state entropy, does not undergo any finite-temperature ground state selection by an order-by-disorder mechanism, and exhibits algebraically decaying correlations. Demonstrating these properties requires performing a Monte Carlo simulation of the statistical Boltzmann distribution. As is the general case with Ising models, single spin flip Markov chain updates face exponentially small acceptance rates at low temperature. This problem is doubly compounded in the present fracton spin liquid by the highly correlated sequence of spin flips required to achieve a vacuum-to-vacuum cage move and the associated high energy barrier. In an ice model, one only pays the price of creating a pair of spinons, after which they can undergo diffusive random walks at zero energy cost until they meet again and annihilate. In the fracton CSL, a single spin flip creates two lineons, which cannot move off of a chain; instead, they can only be split as in Fig. 4(c), costing additional energy. Even after a number of lineons are created, they can only be recombined if their associated lines intersect in trios, to form a cage net such as those in Fig. 6(a,b). This makes single spin flip Monte Carlo untenable for low-temperature simulations.

To overcome this problem, we have developed a highly efficient cluster algorithm capable of generating cage-nets like the one shown in Fig. 6(b). The algorithm generalizes the graph decomposition algorithm developed by Otsuka for constructing string-nets to simulate spin ice [77], itself a generalization of the Swendsen-Wang algorithm [138]. In order to construct cage-nets, the algorithm operates by “breaking up” each octahedron into straight segments, corners, or endpoints, designed to decompose each spin configuration into networks of straight segments which may either terminate in trios or have open ends. At zero temperature, open ends are forbidden and only closed cage-nets can be created, such as the one shown in Fig. 6(b), while at finite temperatures these cages can have open ends, creating or destroying lineons. A detailed explanation of the algorithm is provided in Appendix E.

The thermodynamic results of the simulations using the cluster algorithm are presented in Fig. 6(c), which shows the temperature dependence of the specific heat and entropy. The specific heat exhibits a smooth Schottky-like peak with a maximum near T/J∼0.6\cramped{T/J\sim 0.6}, corresponding to the depopulation of lineon quasiparticles at low temperatures. We find no evidence of any sharp anomaly that might suggest a phase transition, with the specific heat curve exhibiting no quantitative changes with system size, as shown in the inset of Fig. 6(c). The entropy, obtained by integrating the specific heat (Appendix F), demonstrates extensive degeneracy at zero temperature, with a rather large entropy per spin of approximately 0.1176​(2)\cramped{0.1176(2)}. For comparison, we also compute a Pauling-type estimate as follows: viewed as a vertex model on the cubic lattice with 26=642^{6}=64 total allowed vertex configurations, the ground states allow 10 vertex configurations (eight T1​gT_{1g} ground states plus two A1​uA_{1u} ground states); treating these constraints as independent, the Pauling estimate of the number of ground states of the entire system is Ω≈2Ne​(10/64)Nv\cramped{\Omega\approx 2^{N_{e}}(10/64)^{N_{v}}}, where NeN_{e} is the number of edges (equal to the number of spins) and NvN_{v} is the number of vertices (equal to a third of the number of spins), giving an estimate of the zero-temperature entropy per spin of ln⁡Ω/Ne≈0.074\ln\Omega/N_{e}\approx 0.074 1414 14 The Pauling entropy is expected to give a lower bound on the ground state entropy because it overcounts the single-vertex constraints by treating them as independent, while some constraints are redundant when considering larger clusters. Corrections could be obtained systematically through the so-called numerical linked cluster expansion (NLC) [196]. .

V.3 Rank-2 Tensor CSL: U(1) X-cube Model

By writing the Hamiltonian as in Eq. 10, it is clear that the ground states satisfy a set of microscopic local constraints on each octahedron o\mathrm{o}, given by

Qox​x=Qoy​y=Qoz​z=0,Q_{\mathrm{o}}^{xx}=Q_{\mathrm{o}}^{yy}=Q_{\mathrm{o}}^{zz}=0, (18)

i.e. zero EuE_{u} quadrupole moment of the local spin configuration. We can alternatively express the three diagonal components of QQ as the (x2−y2)(x^{2}-y^{2}) and equivalent quadrupole moment components in the three planes,

qoz\displaystyle q^{z}_{\mathrm{o}} =Qox​x−Qoy​y,\displaystyle=Q^{xx}_{\mathrm{o}}-Q^{yy}_{\mathrm{o}},
qoy\displaystyle q^{y}_{\mathrm{o}} =Qoz​z−Qox​x,\displaystyle=Q^{zz}_{\mathrm{o}}-Q^{xx}_{\mathrm{o}},
qox\displaystyle q^{x}_{\mathrm{o}} =Qoy​y−Qoz​z.\displaystyle=Q^{yy}_{\mathrm{o}}-Q^{zz}_{\mathrm{o}}. (19)

These are not linearly independent—∑αqoα=0\cramped{\sum_{\alpha}q^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{o}}=0}, reflecting Tr⁡[Q]=0\cramped{\Tr[Q]=0}—and so form an over-complete basis for the two EuE_{u} degrees of freedom, but with the advantage that the three directions are treated equivalently. Explicitly, in terms of the local moment directions 𝒅^i=Siz​𝒛^i\hat{\bm{d}}_{i}=S_{i}^{z}\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} these can be written as

qoz∝[dx​(𝒓o+δ​𝒙^)−dx​(𝒓o−δ​𝒙^)]\displaystyle q^{z}_{\mathrm{o}}\propto[d^{x}(\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}}+\delta\hat{\bm{x}})-d^{x}(\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}}-\delta\hat{\bm{x}})] (20)
−[dy​(𝒓o+δ​𝒚^)−dy​(𝒓o−δ​𝒚^)],\displaystyle-[d^{y}(\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}}+\delta\hat{\bm{y}})-d^{y}(\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}}-\delta\hat{\bm{y}})],

and similarly for qoxq_{\mathrm{o}}^{x} and qoyq_{\mathrm{o}}^{y}, where 𝒓o\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}} is the location of the center of the octahedron o\mathrm{o} and δ\delta is the distance from the center of an octahedron to a corner. Coarse-graining by taking the limit δ→0\delta\to 0 in Eq. 20, we obtain the following three Gauss laws relating the coarse-grained quadrupolar charge density 𝓺\bm{\mathscr{q}} to the dipole moment density field 𝓓\bm{\mathscr{D}},

𝓆z\displaystyle\mathscr{q}_{z} =∂x𝒟x−∂y𝒟y,\displaystyle=\partial_{x}\mathscr{D}_{x}-\partial_{y}\mathscr{D}_{y},
𝓆y\displaystyle\mathscr{q}_{y} =∂z𝒟z−∂x𝒟x,\displaystyle=\partial_{z}\mathscr{D}_{z}-\partial_{x}\mathscr{D}_{x},
𝓆x\displaystyle\mathscr{q}_{x} =∂y𝒟y−∂z𝒟z,\displaystyle=\partial_{y}\mathscr{D}_{y}-\partial_{z}\mathscr{D}_{z}, (21)

which is the continuum equivalent of Eq. 19. These three constraints can be put in the form of a tensor gauge theory by rearranging the components of the dipole moment vector field into a hollow symmetric rank-2 tensor “electric” field ℰ\mathscr{E}, and writing the Gauss constraint as

𝓆α=ϵα​β​γ​∂βℰγ​α=0with ℰ=(0𝒟z𝒟y𝒟z0𝒟x𝒟y𝒟x0),\mathscr{q}_{\alpha}=\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\partial_{\beta}\mathscr{E}_{\gamma\alpha}=0\quad\text{with }\quad\mathscr{E}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathscr{D}_{z}&\mathscr{D}_{y}\\ \mathscr{D}_{z}&0&\mathscr{D}_{x}\\ \mathscr{D}_{y}&\mathscr{D}_{x}&0\end{pmatrix}, (22)

where ϵα​β​γ\epsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma} is the Levi-Civita symbol and only the β\beta and γ\gamma indices are contracted. Summing over α\alpha, one finds that ∑α𝓆α=0\cramped{\sum_{\alpha}\mathscr{q}_{\alpha}=0}, reflecting the analogous redundancy of the microscopic equivalents, Eq. 19, showing that there are only two linearly independent charges—the two components of the EuE_{u} quadrupole moment.

The Gauss law in Eq. 22 is known to encode the gauge structure of the U(1) X-cube field theory [140, 141, 117, 80] (called the “A^\hat{A} theory” in Ref. [140]). The quantum X-cube model, originally introduced in its ℤ2\mathbbm{Z}_{2} version by Vijay, Haah, and Fu in Ref. [80], is a minimal lattice model realizing fracton topological order, and can be viewed as a generalization the ℤ2\mathbbm{Z}_{2} toric code model which realizes Abelian topological order [142]. As a type of lattice gauge theory, the X-cube model can straightforwardly extended to ℤN\mathbbm{Z}_{N} and U(1) gauge groups [143, 141, 140, 144]. Its ℤN\mathbbm{Z}_{N} incarnations are often presented in terms of a stabilizer Hamiltonian containing two sets of commuting operators—“star operators” at each vertex and “cube operators” for each cube [80, 117, 145, 146]. The octochlore fracton CSL we have been discussing in this section realizes a classical version of the U(1) X-cube model. In the classical model (viewed as the classical limit of a quantum spin-1/2 model), the local constraints given in Eqs. 18 and 19 enforce that the electric field (whose role is played by the spin-1/2 SzS^{z} operators) has zero (a2−b2)(\cramped{a^{2}-b^{2}}) moment in each plane at each vertex (a≠b∈{x,y,z}\cramped{a\neq b\in\{x,y,z\}}), which are equivalent to the constraints enforced by the star operators in the X-cube models. The cube operators, on the other hand, correspond to spin-flipping operators implementing the cube flip shown in Fig. 6(a), which are absent in the classical Hamiltonian.

The correspondence can be made precise as follows: in a U(1) lattice gauge theory the electric field E^\hat{E} takes integer values on each link of the lattice. Let q^vz=(Δx​E^−Δy​E^)v\cramped{\hat{q}^{z}_{v}=(\Delta_{x}\hat{E}-\Delta_{y}\hat{E})_{v}} denote the (x2−y2)\smash{\cramped{(x^{2}-y^{2})}} moment of the electric field configuration at vertex vv, where Δx\Delta_{x} denotes the discrete finite-difference along the xx direction, etc. (compare to Eq. 20). In the matter-free theory, the operators implementing U(1) gauge transformations are A^vα​(θ)=exp⁡(i​θ​q^vα)\cramped{\hat{A}_{v}^{\alpha}(\theta)=\exp(i\theta\hat{q}^{\alpha}_{v})}. In the ℤN\mathbbm{Z}_{N} equivalent gauge theories, where θ\theta is restricted to be a multiple of 2​π/N2\pi/N, these are generated by powers of A^vα=exp⁡(i​2​π​q^vα/N)\cramped{\hat{A}_{v}^{\alpha}=\exp(i2\pi\hat{q}^{\alpha}_{v}/N)} [147], called star operators. In the theory with matter, these operators measure the amount of electric charge at vertex vv. The octochlore X-cube CSL realizes the U(1) version, but with a half-odd-integer-valued electric field, which is further constrained to the values E^=±1/2\cramped{\hat{E}=\pm 1/2} on each link because the spin-1/2 operators S^z\hat{S}^{z} plays the role of E^\hat{E} [54].

In the quantum X-cube models, spin flips violate two of the three star stabilizers at a single vertex, creating lineon quasiparticles restricted to move in one direction [80]. This also happens in the CSL: flipping a spin along the zz-axis generates qox=−qoy≠0q^{x}_{\mathrm{o}}=-q^{y}_{\mathrm{o}}\neq 0 on the two neighboring octahedra; each of these quasiparticles therefore carries (z2−x2)\cramped{(z^{2}-x^{2})} and (z2−y2)\cramped{(z^{2}-y^{2})} quadrupolar charge, summing to an overall uniaxial (3​z2−r2)(3z^{2}-r^{2}) quadrupolar charge; as we demonstrated previously, these are lineon quasiparticles which are constrained to move along the zz axis. Furthermore, in the X-cube models the three star operators at each vertex multiply to the identity, enforcing that the lineon quasiparticles annihilate in trios [146], which in the classical model corresponds to the statement that ∑αqoα=0\cramped{\sum_{\alpha}q_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha}=0}, or equivalently that Tr⁡[Qo]=0\Tr[Q_{\mathrm{o}}]=0. To our knowledge, it has not been previously noted that the lineon quasiparticles of the X-cube model carry quadrupolar charge but this fact is clear in our treatment of the Hamiltonian using multipoles 1515 15 This fact is indirectly implied by the field theory construction of Ref. [140], which assumes that the Noether charges and currents of a global U(1) symmetry transform in a given irrep of the tetrahedral group S4≃Td⊆SO⁡(3)S_{4}\simeq T_{d}\subseteq\mathrm{SO}(3), then gauges that symmetry to obtain a tensor gauge theory. The Gauss law Eq. 22 corresponds to the “A^\hat{A}” theory, whose charges transform in the two-dimensional irrep of S4S_{4}, which descends from the 5-dimensional symmetric tensor (quadrupole) irrep of SO(3). . In the classical model, we have another route to understand this quadrupolar charge via the spinon condensation mechanism explained in Section IV.2. As illustrated in Fig. 3(h), a single spinon carries a uniaxial quadrupolar charge and an A1​uA_{1u} monopolar charge. At the X-cube point, the triple-spinon bound state condensation corresponds to condensing the monopolar charge into the vacuum, so it is no longer conserved; the X-cube quasiparticles retain a conserved quadrupole component, and are restricted to move along the uniaxial director axis.

V.4 Nodal Lines and Spectroscopic Signatures

As discussed in Section III.1, classical spin liquids are usually associated with a set of zero-energy flat bands in the spectrum of the interaction matrix sharing a topological band touching with the dispersing bands [31, 32, 42, 33, 149]. The flat bands give rise to characteristic diffuse patterns in reciprocal space structure factors, while the band touchings give rise to “pinched” singular features reflecting power-law decay correlations in direct space [110, 7]. These pinched features are experimentally detectable in neutron scattering experiments, and can be resolved most clearly using polarization analysis [150], as was famously done in Ho2​Ti2​O7\text{Ho}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{Ti}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{7}}} [21].

The bands of the interaction matrix of Eq. 10 are shown in Fig. 7(a) for the (h​k​0)\cramped{(hk0)} plane in the vicinity of the zone center (see Appendix C for details). Since there are three spins per primitive unit cell, there are three bands. One of three bands (gray) is flat, with both dispersing bands (orange, blue) touching it at the zone center. One of the dispersing bands (orange) is degenerate with the flat band along the {00​h}\{00h\} lines of reciprocal space, a situation referred to as a “nodal line spin liquid” [39, 49]. The origin of these nodal lines follows from real-space topological redundancies in the constraints [34]. In terms of the charges qoαq_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha} defined in Eq. 19, the Hamiltonian Eq. 10 has the form H~∝∑o|𝒒o|2\cramped{\widetilde{H}\propto\sum_{\mathrm{o}}|\bm{q}_{\mathrm{o}}|^{2}}, so ground states satisfy the constraint qoα=0\cramped{q_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha}=0} on every octahedron, with one octahedron per primitive cell. For a system of L3L^{3} unit cells, this appears to impose two independent constraints per cell (since ∑αqoα=0\cramped{\sum_{\alpha}q_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha}=0})—zero (3​z2−r2)(3z^{2}-r^{2}) moment and zero (x2−y2)(x^{2}-y^{2}) moment. Naively, this yields 2​L32L^{3} quadratic constraints, corresponding to two dispersing bands, leaving L3L^{3} unconstrained degrees of freedom forming a single flat band. However, this local counting overlooks global redundancies in a periodic system which reduce the number of linearly independent constraints and enforce zero-energy touchings between the flat and dispersive bands [34]. In particular, for every constant-zz plane pzp_{z}, one has ∑o∈pzqoz=0\sum_{\mathrm{o}\in p_{z}}q_{\mathrm{o}}^{z}=0, with analogous relations for constant-xx and constant-yy planes. This gives 3​L3L apparent redundancies, one per lattice plane, which give rise to extra zero modes along the nodal line touchings—LL along each of the (h​00)(h00), (0​h​0)(0h0), and (00​h)(00h) lines. This actually over-counts the redundancies by one, corresponding to the intersection of the three nodal lines at the zone center. Summing the planar redundancies over all planes is equivalent to summing the local identities ∑αqoα=0\cramped{\sum_{\alpha}q_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha}=0} over all octahedra, so the number of independent redundancies is 3​L−13L-1. The total number of zero modes is therefore L3+(3​L−1)\cramped{L^{3}+(3L-1)}, which we can break down as (cf. Fig. 7(a)): L3L^{3} modes in the flat band, 3×(L−1)\smash{\cramped{3\times(L-1)}} modes along the nodal lines away from the zone center and, finally, the two remaining modes that correspond to the zone center where both dispersive bands touching the flat band.

The nodal line singularities should give rise to characteristic “pinch lines” in reciprocal space correlation functions [39, 32]. However, in general the full structure of these singular features need not necessarily reflected in the spin structure factor (the Fourier transform of ⟨Siz​Sjz⟩\langle S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\rangle summed over all sites, see Appendix C). Indeed, like some other known examples [45, 42], that is the case here—the spin structure factor (not shown) does not exhibit pinch lines. However, their signatures are visible in neutron scattering structure factors, which refine the spin structure factor by weighting the contribution from different sublattices inequivalently depending on the wavevector (Appendix C). They appear as singular features along a grid of lines in reciprocal space parameterized as {2​n,2​m,l}\{2n,2m,l\}, where n,mn,m are integers and ll varies continuously. The singular nature of the nodal lines is most readily revealed by taking a reciprocal-space plane that intersects them transversely, rather than one in which they lie. Planes orthogonal to the (111)(111) directions are therefore particularly useful because they can cut through all three sets of lines at once, especially the one that cuts through the zone center where all three lines intersect, as illustrated in the inset of Fig. 7(b). We compute the unpolarized neutron structure factor in this plane using both the self-consistent Gaussian approximation (SCGA, Appendix C) and Monte Carlo, shown in Fig. 7(b). This reveals a characteristic pinch point pattern, including multi-fold pinches characteristic of higher-rank spin liquids [151]. Further refinement is in principle possible using polarization techniques [21]. For example, Fig. 7(c) shows the calculated spin-flip (SF) and non-spin-flip (NSF) channel cross sections [21, 150, 152].

This concludes our study of the X-cube CSL. It is worth comparing the relative simplicity of classical X-cube CSL identified here to other models considered in the literature. These include models with up to twelve-spin interactions [80], highly fine-tuned interactions up to fifth-nearest-neighbor [79, 78], special anisotropic spin interactions [153], or multiple spins per site [154]. While the octochlore fracton CSL may not be realistic from a materials perspective, in the sense that the second-neighbor interaction is twice the first-neighbor interaction strength, it is perhaps the simplest model for fracton spin liquidity so far explored. Indeed it is likely the minimal possible extension of spin ice (which only requires a single nearest-neighbor interaction on the pyrochlore lattice) to a fracton spin liquid. We proceed next to explore the last part of the phase diagram, directly opposite to the X-cube CSL point, where the ground state may be viewed as a maximal packing of the quadrupolar-charged X-cube lineon quasiparticles.

VI Spin Nematic Phase (𝑬𝒖⊞𝑨𝟏​𝒖\bm{E_{u}\boxplus A_{1u}})

We turn now to the remaining portion of the phase diagram, the Eu⊞A1​u\cramped{E_{u}\boxplus A_{1u}} phase, indicated by the blue-green hatched arc on the bottom right of the phase diagram in Fig. 1(f). As we will show, in this region of the phase diagram the ground state manifold is subextensively degenerate. This gives rise to interesting magnetic frustration physics intermediate between spin liquids and ordered phases—a spin nematic phase exhibiting two-stage dimensional reduction upon decreasing temperature.

VI.1 Fracton Crystal Ground States and Accidental Subsystem Symmetries

This phase contains the point directly opposite to the X-cube fracton CSL point (Section V), whose Hamiltonian is −H~X-cube-\widetilde{H}_{\text{X-cube}} (Eq. 10). At the single-octahedron level, ground states in this phase must be built from the fragmented quadrupolar-plus-monopolar configurations in Fig. 2(b). These configurations maximize the EuE_{u} quadrupole moment locally, meaning that they maximize the number of X-cube lineon quasiparticles on every site. This is analogous to the AIAO phase, which sits across from the spin ice CSL and whose ground states maximize the number of monopoles on every octahedron. Correspondingly, we can view ground states of this phase as maximal packings of X-cube fractons. To see this explicitly, we construct a representative ground state from a uniform tiling of the fragmented configuration from Fig. 2(b). There are six such states related by symmetry, an example of which is shown in Fig. 8(a). In the same way that the single octahedron can be decomposed into fragmented EuE_{u} and A1​uA_{1u} components (cf Fig. 2(b)), these states can be decomposed into a linear combination of a maximal packing of staggered quadrupole moments, as shown in Fig. 8(b), and staggered monopole moments, as shown in Fig. 8(c). The A1​uA_{1u} component in Fig. 8(c) corresponds to a close-packed staggered arrangement of single-charge monopoles, and can therefore be viewed as a monopole crystal [91, 155]. Correspondingly, we may view the EuE_{u} component of this decomposition in Fig. 8(b) as forming a fracton crystal.

These states saturate the EuE_{u} order parameter, Eq. 13, with Tr⁡[Q2]=1\cramped{\Tr[Q^{2}]=1}. They also have a sizeable A1​uA_{1u} order parameter, Eq. 11, with |ϕ|=1/3\cramped{|\phi|=1/3}, owing to the fragmentation of the single-octahedron states (Section II.2). We can further extract the two linearly independent components of the tensor EuE_{u} order parameter as

Q3​c2−r2\displaystyle Q_{3c^{2}-r^{2}} =16​(2​Qc​c−Qa​a−Qb​b),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\left(2Q^{cc}-Q^{aa}-Q^{bb}\right), (23)
Qa2−b2\displaystyle Q_{a^{2}-b^{2}} =12​(Qa​a−Qb​b),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(Q^{aa}-Q^{bb}\right),

with a,b,c,∈{x,y,z}a,b,c,\in\{x,y,z\}, where Q3​c2−r2\smash{Q_{3c^{2}-r^{2}}} measures uniaxiality along the cc direction and Qa2−b2\smash{Q_{a^{2}-b^{2}}} measures biaxiality in the perpendicular a​bab-plane. The ground states illustrated in Fig. 8(a) maximize Q3​c2−r2\smash{Q_{3c^{2}-r^{2}}} while having Qa2−b2=0\smash{\cramped{Q_{a^{2}-b^{2}}=0}}, so we characterize these as uniaxial nematic states—they break global rotational symmetry from cubic to tetragonal, singling out the cc-axis as the uniaxial director axis (a state is uniaxial if two eigenvalues of QQ are degenerate; since QQ is a diagonal matrix its eigenvalues are just its diagonal elements) 1616 16 Our use of the term “nematic” should be distinguished from the more common examples of spin nematicity in quantum spin models with spin quantum number S>1/2S>1/2 (including classical S→∞\cramped{S\to\infty} models) which are characterized by lack of time reversal symmetry breaking, so ⟨Siα⟩=0\langle S_{i}^{\alpha}\rangle=0, but breaking of spin or lattice rotational symmetry as measured by on-site quadrupole operators Qiα​β=(Siα​Siβ−(1/3)​|𝑺i|2​δα​β)\smash{\cramped{Q_{i}^{\alpha\beta}=(S_{i}^{\alpha}S_{i}^{\beta}-(1/3)|\bm{S}_{i}|^{2}\delta_{\alpha\beta})}} [107]. The classical Ising spin nematic phase we identify breaks both time-reversal symmetry and lattice rotation, but preserves the combination of time-reversal and inversion. . We will refer to these as uniaxial fracton crystal ground states.

While the six uniaxial fracton crystal states are the simplest ground states constructed from a uniform tiling of the single-octahedron ground states, the complete ground state manifold is much larger. To demonstrate this, first note that for each single-octahedron ground state [Fig. 2(b)] antipodal pairs of spins are anti-aligned. It follows that any state constructed from these single-octahedron configurations must consist of antiferromagnetically polarized chains, with each chain in one of its two Néel-polarized states. Let us therefore define a Néel order parameter 𝒩𝖼\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}} for each chain 𝖼\mathsf{c} in terms of the local moment directions 𝒅^i=Siz​𝒛^i\hat{\bm{d}}_{i}=S_{i}^{z}\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} as

𝒩𝖼=(−1)𝖼​1L​∑i∈𝖼(−1)i​𝒅^i⋅𝒆^𝖼.\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=(-1)^{\mathsf{c}}\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i\in\mathsf{c}}(-1)^{i}\hat{\bm{d}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{c}}. (24)

Here, 𝒆^𝖼∈{𝒙^,𝒚^,𝒛^}\hat{\bm{e}}_{\mathsf{c}}\in\{\hat{\bm{x}},\hat{\bm{y}},\hat{\bm{z}}\} is the direction of the chain and LL is the number of spins in the chain. The sign (−1)i(-1)^{i} alternates along the chain so that 𝒩𝖼\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}} measures the staggered magnetization, while the sign (−1)𝖼(-1)^{\mathsf{c}} alternates along the two sublattices of the square lattice formed by the chains when viewed along their length, chosen so that the “all-out” state correspond to 𝒩𝖼=+1\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=+1 on every chain. The uniaxial fracton crystal ground state shown in Fig. 8(a) differs from the “all-out” state by flipping every chain along the zz axis—it has 𝒩𝖼=−1\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=-1} for cc-oriented chains (colored blue) and 𝒩𝖼=+1\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=+1} for aa- and bb-oriented chains (colored red).

We can deduce a simple rule that is satisfied if and only if a state is a ground state: all chains must be Néel polarized, and at the intersection of three chains the polarizations are not all the same (i.e., two blue and one red or vice versa), guaranteeing that the local octahedral configuration is of the form ±(c2−a2−b2)\cramped{\pm(c^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2})} (cf. Fig. 2(b)). In particular, starting from the uniaxial fracton crystal state with uniaxial director along the cc-axis, as in Fig. 8(a), we can flip a single chain in any a​bab-plane. We show in Fig. 8(d) the result of flipping a single bb-oriented chain. Once we have flipped such a chain, we can also flip any parallel chain in the same plane, as shown in Fig. 8(e). However, we cannot flip an orthogonal chain in the same plane, which would violate the ground state rule by creating an intersection of three chains with the same 𝒩𝖼\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}, i.e. an all-in or all-out octahedron. In each plane orthogonal to the cc-axis, therefore, we are free to flip all chains along either the aa-axis or the bb-axis, but not both. Once a single chain along the aa-axis has been flipped, no bb-oriented chains can be flipped within the same plane, and vice-versa. The choice of which direction to flip chains can be chosen independently in every a​bab-plane, as illustrated in Fig. 8(f,g). Overall, this gives a subextensive ground state degeneracy scaling as 2L2\smash{2^{L^{2}}}.

This situation is reminiscent of the frustrated chains phase discussed in Section IV, which also exhibits zero-energy chain flips and corresponding subextensive ground state degeneracy. However, here the ability to flip chains is significantly constrained, because flipping chains along the aa- or bb-axes in a single plane are mutually incompatible. To cleanly define the accidental symmetries, we must divide the ground state manifold into sectors labeled by a choice of either the aa- or bb-axis for each plane orthogonal to the uniaxial director cc-axis 1717 17 There are also ground states which do not live in these sectors—for example, starting from the state in Fig. 8(a) flip all chains in one b​cbc-plane, then cc-axis chains in that plane can be flipped, and all bb-axis chains can be flipped. However, these ground states are not naturally reached from the uniaxial states and do not appear to influence the low-temperature behavior, cf. Section VI.3. . Within each such ground state sector, flipping chains along the chosen axes is an accidental subsystem symmetry. As we will see, at low temperatures the system spontaneously will select one such sector.

It is important to draw a key distinction between the zero-energy chain-flips in this portion of the phase diagram compared to those which occur in the T1​gT_{1g} frustrated chains phase. In the frustrated chains phase, the chain-flips are zero modes arising from the flat planar degeneracy of the interaction matrix, in the sense explained in Section III.1. In the Eu⊞A1​uE_{u}\boxplus A_{1u} phase, by contrast, the ground states are not zero-energy states because the fragmented ground states necessarily mix the positive-energy A1​uA_{1u} irrep with the zero-energy EuE_{u} irrep. Consequently, the zero-energy locus of the interaction matrix is not a good guide to the low-energy physics of this phase. As listed in Table 1, the interaction matrix has zero-energy flat lines in reciprocal space, which only imply zero modes which flip entire planes of spins. Indeed, such planar zero modes do exist—if an entire plane has (a2−b2)\cramped{(a^{2}-b^{2})}-type order, such as the a​cac and b​cbc planes in Fig. 8(a), then such a plane can always be flipped at zero energy cost, which is the analog of flipping a polarized chain in the T1​gT_{1g} frustrated chains phase. However, the chain-based flips in the ground state manifold discussed above and illustrated in Fig. 8(d-g) arise as a consequence of fragmentation, rather than as zero modes of the interaction matrix. In particular, they arise because the fragmented ground states are locally of the form c2−a2−b2c^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2} on each octahedron; flipping an aa-chain changes the configuration to c2+a2−b2c^{2}+a^{2}-b^{2}, which is still a fragmented ground state. Therefore, the chain-based flips in the ground state manifold are accidental symmetries—symmetries of the ground state manifold which are not symmetries of the Hamiltonian—rather than exact zero modes.

Unlike exact zero modes, accidental symmetries only act within the ground-state manifold and are generically expected to be broken by order-by-disorder [93]. Nevertheless, accidental symmetries acting on one-dimensional chains have particularly strong consequences because they imply that the minimal excitations above the ordered ground states are deconfined quasiparticles (1D domain walls) moving along the chains, which carry enormous configurational entropy. This is much more impactful on the low-energy physics than zero modes acting on two-dimensional manifolds, which implies the existence of string-like 2D domain walls, which are confined by their string tension. In the case at hand, since the chains are all Néel ordered in the ground state, the accidental chain-based symmetries flipping chains imply the existence of fractionalized antiferro-spinon excitations—domain walls between the Néel domains on a single chain. This is illustrated in Fig. 9, which shows two Néel domains on a single chain, meeting at a domain wall. Just like ferro-spinons, these low-energy quasiparticles are deconfined, they can be moved along the chain at zero energy cost by flipping a series of spins. Notably, however, this deconfinement requires that the spins surrounding the chain are frozen in their ground state configuration, and is therefore only operative at very low temperatures when defects are dilute. Flipping spins along the uniaxial director axis is not an accidental symmetry, implying that the antiferro-spinons cannot move along this axis without paying energy proportional to their separation—they are confined along the director (cc-axis). Furthermore, because the accidental subsystem symmetries can only perform unconstrained flips of parallel chains in each plane, the deconfinement of antiferro-spinons can only occur in one of two directions in each plane. This suggests that the low-temperature physics will involve the spontaneous selection of one of the above-defined ground state sectors, driven by a free energy gain from deconfinement of antiferro-spinons.

VI.2 Transition to Uniaxial Nematic Order

We now investigate the finite-temperature behavior of the system in the Eu⊞A1​uE_{u}\boxplus A_{1u} region of the phase diagram using Monte Carlo simulations. Despite the subextensive degeneracy of the ground-state manifold discussed above, upon cooling, the system first undergoes a conventional finite-temperature transition out of the paramagnet and into a uniaxial nematic phase, signaled by a prominent sharp peak in the specific heat. The corresponding transition temperatures are marked in the phase diagram Fig. 1(f). The maximum critical temperature occurs near the point in the phase diagram directly opposite the X-cube CSL, which is labeled “fully packed fractons” in Fig. 1(f). We therefore focus on this representative point, whose thermodynamic behavior is qualitatively characteristic of the entire phase. Figure 10 shows the temperature evolution of (a) the specific heat, (b) the multipole order parameters defined in Eqs. 11, 12 and 13, and (c) the magnitudes of the eigenvalues of the quadrupole tensor order parameter. The specific heat displays a prominent peak at Tcuni/J≈1.56\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}}/J\approx 1.56, indicating a thermodynamic phase transition. We first focus on the physics of this transition and the phase just below it. A second transition occurs at lower temperature, which will be analyzed separately in Section VI.3.

To identify the symmetry of the ordered phase, we examine the multipolar order parameters and the eigenvalues of the quadrupole tensor. Just below Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}}, Fig. 10(b) shows that the EuE_{u} order parameter develops rapidly, while the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter exhibits a weaker activation. Figure 10(c) shows that two eigenvalues of the quadrupole tensor are degenerate, demonstrating that this transition spontaneously breaks the cubic rotational symmetry down to a tetragonal subgroup. This characterizes this intermediate-temperature regime as a uniaxial nematic phase.

The formation of this intermediate-temperature uniaxial phase can be understood from a Landau free energy expansion in terms of the scalar A1​uA_{1u} and EuE_{u} order parameters,

F⁡[ϕ,Q]\displaystyle F[\phi,Q] =rE​Tr⁡[Q2]+rA​ϕ2+w​ϕ​Tr⁡[Q3]\displaystyle=r_{E}\Tr[Q^{2}]+r_{A}\phi^{2}+w\,\phi\Tr[Q^{3}]
+g​ϕ2​Tr⁡[Q2]+uA​ϕ4+uE​Tr⁡[Q2]2+⋯\displaystyle+g\phi^{2}\Tr[Q^{2}]+u_{A}\phi^{4}+u_{E}\Tr[Q^{2}]^{2}+\cdots (25)

where the ellipses denote terms involving the T1​gT_{1g} dipole order parameter as well as sixth-order and higher terms 1818 18 Up to fourth order the only allowed T1​gT_{1g} couplings are rT​|𝑫|2r_{T}|\bm{D}|^{2}, uT​|𝑫|4u_{T}|\bm{D}|^{4}, g′​|𝑫|2​ϕ2g^{\prime}|\bm{D}|^{2}\phi^{2}, g′′​|𝑫|2​Tr⁡[Q2]g^{\prime\prime}|\bm{D}|^{2}\Tr[Q^{2}], with no linear-cubic couplings. We expect both rA,rT>0r_{A},r_{T}>0 at the transition since these irreps are gapped in the microscopic Hamiltonian, but with rA≪rT\cramped{r_{A}\ll r_{T}} since the c2−a2−b2\cramped{c^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2}} single-octahedron fragmented ground state configurations, Fig. 2(b), carry an A1​uA_{1u} component. . While we will not embark into a detailed analysis of the critical behavior, the form of the free energy explains the principal features observed in Monte Carlo simulations. Microscopically, the energetics of an isolated octahedron favor states with dominant EuE_{u} character, making quadrupolar order the primary instability upon cooling. The linear-cubic coupling w​ϕ​Tr⁡[Q3]w\phi\Tr[Q^{3}] then induces a secondary A1​uA_{1u} component when EuE_{u} order develops, naturally accounting for the simultaneous activation of both order parameters in Fig. 10(b) and for the comparatively weaker magnitude of the A1​uA_{1u} signal 1919 19 Indeed the sign of ww must be fixed microscopically by the fact that the signs of these two contributions are opposite—the (c2−a2−b2)(c^{2}-a^{2}-b^{2}) state in Fig. 2(b) has Tr⁡[Qo3]>0\cramped{\Tr[Q_{\mathrm{o}}^{3}]>0} and ϕo<0\cramped{\phi_{\mathrm{o}}<0}, implying that w>0\cramped{w>0}). . Furthermore, the minima of this quartic free energy functional always correspond to uniaxial orders (of 3​c2−r2\cramped{3c^{2}-r^{2}} type), which have Tr⁡[Q3]≠0\cramped{\Tr[Q^{3}]\neq 0}, whereas purely biaxial orders (of a2−b2\cramped{a^{2}-b^{2}} type) have Tr⁡[Q3]=0\cramped{\Tr[Q^{3}]=0} and are only selected by tuning a sixth-order Tr⁡[Q3]2\Tr[Q^{3}]^{2} term which is irrelevant under scaling 2020 20 We could alternatively define a two-component vector order parameter for the EuE_{u} irrep using Eq. 23, or equivalently a single complex order parameter, q~=Q3​z2−r2+i​Qx2−y2=|q~|​ei​ϑ.\tilde{q}=Q_{3z^{2}-r^{2}}+iQ_{x^{2}-y^{2}}=|\tilde{q}|e^{i\vartheta}. In terms of q~\tilde{q}, we can rewrite the quadrupole tensor invariants as Tr⁡[Q2]=|q~|2\cramped{\Tr[Q^{2}]=|\tilde{q}|^{2}} and Tr⁡[Q3]=|q~|3​cos⁡(3​ϑ)/6\cramped{\Tr[Q^{3}]=|\tilde{q}|^{3}\cos(3\vartheta)}/\sqrt{6}. The six pure-uniaxial ±(3​c2−r2)\cramped{\pm(3c^{2}-r^{2})} order parameters correspond to ϑ∈(2​π/6)​ℤ\cramped{\vartheta\in(2\pi/6)\mathbbm{Z}}, while the six pure-biaxial ±(a2−b2)\cramped{\pm(a^{2}-b^{2})} order parameters with Tr⁡[Q3]=0\cramped{\Tr[Q^{3}]=0} correspond to ϑ∈(2​π/6)​(ℤ+1/2)\cramped{\vartheta\in(2\pi/6)(\mathbbm{Z}+1/2)}. This free energy is then formally equivalent to that describing the development of so-called “ψ2\psi_{2}” (uniaxial) and “ψ3\psi_{3}” (biaxial) orders in anisotropic pyrochlore spin models, in which biaxial states are selected by a (dangerously) irrelevant sixth-order cos⁡(6​ϑ)\cos(6\vartheta) term [123, 36, 3, 16]. The activation of the scalar order parameter has also been observed to occur in the pyrochlore by the same linear-cubic coupling [36]. .

These observations are consistent with a simple microscopic picture: a typical microstate in this phase may be viewed as a thermally disordered version of one of the six uniaxial fracton crystal ground states. In fact, this picture can be directly observed in real-space snapshots taken from Monte Carlo simulations. The key observables that expose the behavior are the chain-based Néel polarizations 𝒩𝖼\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}} (Eq. 24). In Fig. 11 we visualize the values of 𝒩𝖼\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}} for all chains by associating each chain to a point on the surface of a cube. Each panel shows a snapshot of a typical configuration at different temperatures from a single simulation which has been slowly annealed. Blue (red) points on the cube surface indicate chains with 𝒩𝖼<0\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}<0} (𝒩𝖼>0\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}>0}), while white points indicate chains with 𝒩𝖼≈0\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}\approx 0}. Figure 11(a) shows a snapshot above Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}} in the paramagnetic phase, where all of the chain order parameters are nearly zero on every chain in all directions. Figure 11(b) shows a snapshot below the transition to the uniaxial phase: chains along the cc-axis exhibit a large 𝒩𝖼≈−1\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}\approx-1} (blue face of the cube), while the aa- and bb-axis chains exhibit weaker but opposite ordering, 𝒩𝖼∼+0.5\cramped{\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}\sim+0.5} (washed-out red faces). This pattern clearly breaks the rotational symmetry of the cube to a tetragonal subgroup, and is consistent with a thermally disordered version of the uniaxial fracton crystal state state shown in Fig. 8(a), which would produce a cube with one blue face (𝒩𝖼=−1\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=-1) and two red faces (𝒩𝖼=+1\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=+1).

Despite the highly unconventional structure of the ground-state manifold established in Section VI.1, the highest-temperature ordering transition at Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}} is governed primarily by local single-octahedron energetics and appears fairly conventional. The role of the accidental subsystem symmetries only becomes apparent upon further cooling, as we discuss next.

VI.3 Fluctuation-Driven Biaxiality and Dimensional Reduction

As the temperature continues to decrease, the density of gapped excitations diminishes the system begins to approach its ground state manifold, with the uniaxial crystalline structure becoming more rigid. As discussed in Section VI.1 and illustrated in Fig. 8(d-f), the ground state manifold exhibits accidental subsystem symmetries: in each plane orthogonal to the cc-axis, chains parallel to either the aa- or bb-axis can be flipped at zero energy cost, but not both. At the lowest energies, the minimal excitations propagating on top of the uniaxial fracton crystal state are 1D antiferro-spinons, illustrated in Fig. 9. These excitations can in principle deconfine along either the aa- or bb-axis in each plane, implying an instability of the uniaxial fracton crystal ground state at low temperatures.

Indeed, returning to the numerical results in Fig. 10, a second phase transition occurs at a lower temperature Tcbi/J≈0.96\smash{T_{c}^{\text{bi}}}/J\approx 0.96, signaled by a small peak in the specific heat, which is only clearly resolvable for relatively large system sizes—the bottom right inset of Fig. 10(a) shows its weak system size dependence. Despite the weakness of the specific heat response, the low-temperature phase is strikingly characterized by the eigenvalues of the quadrupolar order parameter, Fig. 10(c)—the two degenerate eigenvalues split below Tcbi\smash{T_{c}^{\text{bi}}}, resulting in a biaxial nematic phase, i.e. one with Qa2−b2≠0Q_{a^{2}-b^{2}}\neq 0 (Eq. 23). The real-space snapshot shown in Fig. 11(c) illustrates what is happening: within each plane orthogonal to the cc-axis, chains along either the aa- or bb-axis are polarized with saturated |𝒩𝖼|≈1|\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}|\approx 1, while chains along the third axis have become highly disordered with 𝒩𝖼≈0\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}\approx 0. This is consistent with the deconfinement of antiferro-spinons in each plane along one of the two axes—by the standard Peierls argument, the presence of these deconfined quasiparticles disorders the chains at finite temperature, yielding a large finite-temperature entropy and a significant reduction in free energy, resulting in a fluctuation-driven instability of the uniaxial fracton crystal structure. Such a fluctuation-driven mechanism is a type of order-by-disorder [92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97], but instead of selecting a particular state out of a large ground state manifold, it instead drives spontaneous dimensional reduction—the low temperature behavior is that of decoupled 1D chains which are disordered in the low-temperature limit.

The dimensional reduction to 1D chain behavior is reflected in our numerical observations at the lowest temperature. First, near the transition to the biaxial phase, the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter declines precipitously, as seen in Fig. 10(b). This is consistent with the deconfinement of antiferro-spinons and the disordering of the Néel domains: as shown in Fig. 9, the two Néel domains have opposite patterns of staggered monopole moments, so they tend to cancel each other in their contribution to the scalar A1​uA_{1u} order parameter, which measures the staggered monopole moment. Note that the staggered EuE_{u} moments in the two domains are aligned along two different axes, therefore they do not give canceling contributions to the quadrupole tensor order parameter but rather contribute to two different components of it, giving rise to a net biaxial moment. Second, at the lowest temperatures T/J≲0.5T/J\lesssim 0.5 we see clear features which can be understood as finite-size effects associate with finite-length 1D chains. The inset of Fig. 10(a) shows that the low-temperature decay of the specific heat matches the exact solution for finite-length 1D chains (Appendix D). At the same temperature the order parameters shown in Fig. 10(b,c) begin to behave erratically, most strikingly the A1​uA_{1u} behavior. Figure 11(d) demonstrates that at these temperatures the disordered chains are becoming frozen into one of their two Néel ground states. This occurs when the correlation length of the one-dimensional chains has exceeded the finite system size, giving random athermal contributions to the order parameters. In the thermodynamic limit, the chains can remain disordered at any finite temperature. Altogether our Monte Carlo data confirms that the lowest-temperature physics is that of decoupled chains, making this a realization of spontaneous dimensional reduction [98, 99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104] in a classical Ising model.

Returning to the snapshot shown in Fig. 11(c), it is clear that the biaxial phase also breaks translation symmetry along the direction of the uniaxial director axis. As discussed in Section VI.1, the accidental subsystem symmetries in this system are highly constrained—for each a​bab-plane, chains along either the aa-axis or the bb-axis can be flipped independently, but these two sets of accidental symmetries are mutually incompatible with each other within a given plane. Therefore, the ground state manifold is divided into sectors labeled by a choice of aa- or bb-axis in each plane orthogonal to the uniaxial director, so that within each such sector there is an emergent subsystem symmetry flipping chains along the chosen axes. These accidental symmetries guarantee a massive entropy gain from deconfined quasiparticles, so it is thermodynamically favorable for the system to spontaneously choose one such sector. One expects that thermal fluctuations will split the free energies of the different sectors at finite temperature, generating weak effective inter-plane interactions, mediated by flipping spins along the uniaxial director axis. Because our annealed simulations are cooled through the transition at a finite rate (i.e. non-adiabatically), they do not necessarily find the sector which globally optimizes the free energy. It therefore remains a question as to which sector is chosen in thermodynamic limit, i.e. the extent of effective inter-plane interactions induced by thermal fluctuations.

The simplest scenario one may envisage is that the system selects the uniform sector where the same axis is chosen in every plane, but that is not what is observed in Fig. 11(c). In our annealed Monte Carlo simulations, each independent replica finds a different pattern of plane-dependent rotational symmetry breaking. This is clear from the quantized plateaus reached by the sub-dominant eigenvalues of the quadrupole tensor order parameter shown in Fig. 10(c). We can compute the allowed plateau values as follows: assume that all cc-chains are with 𝒩𝖼=−1\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=-1, and that N∈[0,L]N\in[0,L] of the a​bab-planes are polarized along aa (with 𝒩𝖼=+1\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}=+1) and deconfined along bb (with 𝒩𝖼≈0\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{c}}\approx 0), where LL is the number of planes. Correspondingly, L−NL-N planes are polarized along bb and deconfined along aa. For such a state the quadrupole tensor order parameter, Eq. 13, is given by

Q→32​6​diag​(NL,1−NL,−1).Q\to\frac{3}{2\sqrt{6}}\mathrm{diag}\left(\frac{N}{L},1-\frac{N}{L},-1\right). (26)

Each value of NN gives a different set of plateau values for the two sub-dominant eigenvalues, which are marked in Fig. 10(c) with thin dashed horizontal lines. Different values of NN also give rise to slightly different magnitudes of the EuE_{u} order parameter, which can be seen in Fig. 10(b).

Weak inter-plane correlations are evidenced in the distribution of NN. If the plane polarizations were completely independent, NN would follow a binomial distribution peaked at N=L/2N=L/2. On the right side of Fig. 10(c), we show a histogram of the plateau values of the two subleading eigenvalues taken from 250 annealed simulations, with a binomial distribution superimposed (dashed black line) Small systematic deviations from the binomial distribution are visible: the weight near N=L/2N=L/2 is somewhat suppressed and the distribution is slightly broadened. This result demonstrates measurable but weak correlations between planes and some free energy preference among the different ground state sectors. Determining the nature of the inter-plane interactions and whether they select a specific sector in the thermodynamic limit would require a careful study of system-size dependence of such histograms over significantly more slowly annealed simulations, and comparison to low-temperature series expansions [161], a topic that we leave for future study.

This concludes our study of the spin nematic Eu⊞A1​uE_{u}\boxplus A_{1u} phase. Before closing, we briefly comment on how the physics of this phase relates to similar behavior in other spin models. Spontaneous dimensional reduction and spin nematicity have been conclusively demonstrated in so-called compass models, which are multi-component (continuous) spin models with directional interactions hosting exact chain-based subsystem symmetries [98, 99, 101, 162, 163, 164, 165, 103, 36]. For Ising systems, a somewhat similar model is the Xu-Moore or square-plaquette model, involving four-spin interactions on the square lattice with exact subsystem symmetries [100], but the physics there involves immobile fracton-like excitations.

A model with more closely related physics is the domino model originally studied by Villain et al. in their pioneering work on order-by-disorder [93]. The domino model is a square lattice Ising model with alternating ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic chains, with ferromagnetic inter-chain coupling. Since the Hamiltonian explicitly breaks rotational symmetry, it cannot exhibit spontaneous nematic behavior, but it does host chain-flipping accidental symmetries and correspondingly has subextensive ground state degeneracy. This system is disordered at zero temperature, yet exhibits finite magnetization upon cooling towards zero temperature, a classic example of order-by-disorder—fluctuations in the antiferro-chains generate effective interactions between the ferro-chain, making it entropically favorable for them all to polarize the same way. Drawing insight from the discussion in this Section regarding the octochlore spin nematic phase, one can reinterpret the origin of this behavior: the disorder at zero temperature in the domino model may be viewed result of the lowest-energy excitations being deconfined spinons. However, these spinons need not be deconfined at finite temperature—the ability of a spinon to traverse its chain at zero energy cost is only guaranteed to cost zero energy if the surrounding spins are frozen in their ground state configuration. Thus, fluctuations of those off-chain spins can confine the spinons, or in other words generate a string tension, allowing the system to be ordered at finite temperature. Such a putative string tension would be the analog of the thermally-generated pseudo-goldstone gap in systems with accidental continuous U(1) symmetries [166, 167, 168]. Indeed our thermodynamic data shown in Fig. 10(b) are potentially consistent with the presence of a weak string tension between antiferro-spinons, because the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter does not vanish in the biaxial phase. As illustrated in Fig. 9, the deconfinement of antiferro-spinons on the chains should disorder the Néel domains and thereby fully disorder the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter. The fact that the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter remains small but finite may imply that the disordered chains retain a small but finite Néel order parameter. Given this interpretation, we would then predict that in the thermodynamic limit the disordered chains’ Néel order parameters, and the A1​uA_{1u} order parameter, should remain finite in the biaxial phase but tend towards zero at T=0T=0, corresponding to the vanishing of a (fluctuation-generated string tension between antiferro-spinons. We leave the exploration of such an interesting possibility for future work.

VII Magnetic Octochlore Materials

Having established in detail the phase diagram of the classical Ising Hamiltonian on the octochlore lattice, Eq. 1, in the preceding sections, we now turn to the question of its physical realization. From a materials perspective, the octochlore geometry is realized by the magnetic-moment-bearing sites of anti-perovskite compounds and also in a class of magnetic trivalent rare-earth fluoride insulators. In this section, we survey these two material families, which offer a concrete experimental arena in which the exotic physics harbored by our minimal model may be sought.

VII.1 Rare Earth Anti-Perovskites

The octochlore structure is perhaps best known in the anti-perovskite (or inverse-perovskite) structure, realized in materials with chemical formula R3​AX\text{R}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{AX} [57]. The R ions form the octochlore lattice as shown in Fig. 12(a), with X ions sitting at the centers of octahedra and A ions in the voids between octahedra. Of note, anti-perovskites are typically metallic, with a transition metal ion such as Mn occupying the R site [57]. Placing rare-earth ions on the R site of an ideal insulating anti-perovskite is highly unfavorable—their strong preference for the 3+ oxidation state would require unrealistically large negative charge on the A and X ions to maintain charge neutrality. Therefore rare-earth anti-perovskites should generally be expected to be metallic. If the 4​f4f moments remain strongly localized and unquenched (weak Kondo coupling), RKKY interaction would naturally generate spin-spin exchange in such materials, though not limited to J1J_{1} and J2​aJ_{2a}. Many lanthanide anti-perovskite nitrides have been proposed as stable materials [64]. Indeed a series of metallic rare earth nitrides R3​NIn\text{R}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{NIn} with R a rare earth have been synthesized and characterized [59, 60, 61]. One compound in particular, Ce3​NIn\text{Ce}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{NIn}, was found to exhibit a transition to commensurate antiferromagnetic order with moments aligned along the crystal axes in Ising-like fashion, apparently with each octahedron in the state shown in Fig. 3(d) [62]. Another rare-earth antiperovskite compound, Ho3​InC\text{Ho}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{InC}, was recently reported to have a ground state consisting of a staggered arrangement of the configurations shown in Fig. 3(c), suggested to be stabilized by first and second (including J2​bJ_{2b}) neighbor interactions [65]. In a somewhat different context, the rare earth antiperovskite compound Eu3​PbO\text{Eu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{PbO}, while not having Ising moments, exhibits a rich variety of tunable topological semimetal behaviors [63]. While anti-perovskites may not be an ideal place to realize rare earth octochlore insulators, they are a promising platform for metallic frustrated magnets, which have generated much interest as platforms for the study of exotic quantum criticality [169, 170] and non-Fermi liquid behaviors [6].

VII.2 Rare Earth Octochlore Fluorides

A promising family of insulating materials is AR3​F10\text{AR}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{F}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{10}}} [66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72, 73], with R a trivalent rare earth ion, and A –  – K, Rb, Cs, which realize the octochlore structure as shown in Fig. 12(b). Each rare earth ion sits in a square anti-prism cage of F ions with C4​vC_{4v} symmetry (compare to the distorted cube cage of O ions with D3​dD_{3d} symmetry surrounding each rare earth ion in pyrochlore oxides [171]). Interestingly, and of significant importance to make experimental progress in the study of highly frustrated magnetic materials, these compounds can be grown as single crystals [72, 73]. Chamberlain et al. synthesized the KR3​F10\text{KR}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{F}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{10}}} series with R –  – Dy [67], Er, Yb  [69], each of which likely exhibit a crystal field ground state doublet with predominantly Ising-like moments (KTm3F10 may, given its reported thermodynamics [69], have a nearly-degenerate singlet pair). The compounds with R –  – Ho [70] and Tb [73, 69] have a non-magnetic singlet crystal field ground state, but the remaining Lanthanide rare earth compounds in this series remain promising candidates for interesting frustrated magnetic insulators. It is also possible to substitute K by Rb [68, 70] or Cs [72], yielding additional series in the family. In particular the compound RbSm3​F10\text{RbSm}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{F}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{10}}} has been reported to have Ising moments with no order down to 8 mK [70]. It appears that little further work has been done to study this family as a platform for frustrated magnetism, but the ground work has been laid to explore these compounds in more detail.

Chamberlain et al. reports competition between dipole and exchange couplings in the KR3​F10\text{KR}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{F}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{10}}} compounds they studied [67, 69, 70], which may be favorable for observing spin ice physics of dipolar origin [172] in some of those compounds at low temperatures [58]. In a similar vein as in current efforts devoted to some rare-earth pyrochlore oxides [17, 16, 3], it will be especially interesting to explore whether such compounds with small magnetic moments can be synthesized and whose behavior is governed primarily by exchange couplings as opposed to long-range magnetostatic dipole-dipole interactions. While the second-neighbor J2​aJ_{2a} exchange may be expected to be weaker than first-neighbor J1J_{1} exchange interaction, for lack of an anion ligand mediating a superexchange pathway, making the realization of the fracton CSL and frustrated chains phase potentially challenging, a positive J1J_{1} with a small J2​aJ_{2a} could stabilize either the fragmented spin ice CSL or the spin nematic phase in the phase diagram of Fig. 1(f). Observation of either of these would be a significant achievement in the exploration of frustrated magnetic phenomena in three dimensions. Given advances in crystal growth methods which have been applied intensively to grow large clean single crystals of a variety of pyrochlore compounds [173], and growing interest in non-oxide pyrochlores [174], this family of non-oxide octochlore compounds is a promising avenue for exploring the rich physics discussed in this work.

VIII Discussion

In this work, we have explored in detail the phase diagram of Ising moments on a three-dimensional octochlore lattice, shown in Fig. 1(a), with first-neighbor J1J_{1} and second-neighbor J2​aJ_{2a} interactions inside each octahedron, leveraging the notion of irreducible cluster multipole moments [105] for each octahedron which have played a key role in the study of pyrochlore magnetism [39, 35, 30, 38, 40, 41, 42, 36, 43, 44, 37]. Some of the physics is familiar from the pyrochlore lattice: there is a spin ice string-net classical spin liquid with quasiparticle excitations carrying monopole moments and an all-in/all-out phase whose ground states can be viewed as a fully packaged crystalline arrangement of monopoles. We identified three parts of the phase diagram hosting remarkable frustrated physics without clear precedent: a frustrated chains phase exhibiting a smooth dimensional crossover and quasicritical Kasteleyn-like physics (Section IV); a fracton cage-net CSL that hosts lineon quasiparticle excitations carrying quadrupole moments and realizing a classical X-cube model (Section V); and a spin nematic phase exhibiting spontaneous dimensional reduction (Section VI). The frustrated chains and spin nematic phases exhibit subextensive degeneracies intermediate between spin liquids and ordered phases, and their low-temperature physics is driven by deconfinement of 1D spinon quasiparticles and corresponding emergent subsystem symmetries. Our work opens numerous avenues for further research into the physics of 3D frustrated magnets with Ising moments. Most importantly, it lays the basic foundation for experimental work studying octochlore materials such as those discussed in Section VII. Before concluding, we briefly outline interesting directions for future work building on our results.

VIII.1 Open Questions for the Frustrated Chains Phase

With regard to the classical model studied here, a number of interesting questions remain. A prominent question is the nature of the avoided Kasteleyn-like transitions at the ends of the frustrated chains phase discussed in Section IV.3 where there are at least two key directions to explore. A first would be to characterize the nature of the confinement-deconfinement transition driven by the “string bending energy” described by Eq. 16, which is similar yet distinct from the Kasteleyn transition driven by string tension described by Eq. 15. A second direction would be to study the analogous physics near the fractonic X-cube spin liquid, where we conjecture that a similar avoided crossover occurs in our phase diagram—what is the nature of the Kasteleyn-like confinement transitions out of a fracton spin liquid described by Eq. 17? Furthermore, it is interesting to ask whether the zero-modes of this phase guarantee that there is no phase transition, along the lines of the generalized Elitzur’s theorem of Ref. [99] which guarantees no phase transition for exact chain-based subsystem symmetries.

VIII.2 Open Questions for the Spin Nematic Phase

With regard to the biaxial spin nematic phase discussed in Section VI, we have not determined whether the direction of the secondary axes within the biaxial phase is truly random in different planes. We found evidence for weak inter-plane correlations, but it is an interesting statistical mechanism problem to explore the consequence of these interactions in the thermodynamic limit and whether a particular ordered pattern is selected via order-by-disorder. Furthermore, at the end of Section VI we commented on similarity between the physics of the biaxial phase and the domino model [93], and hypothesized that the antiferro-spinon excitations could be weakly confined by a temperature-dependent string tension analogous to the thermal gap of pseudo-Goldstone bosons in systems with accidental U(1) symmetries [166, 167, 168]. Exploring these issues further could deepen our understanding of order-by-disorder in classical Ising models, examples of which are sparse [93, 96, 175, 176].

VIII.3 Spinon Bound State Condensation Mechanism

In Section IV.2 we showed that the two CSLs in the current model can be viewed as condensates of different bound states of spinons arising from coupled chains. This is similar in spirit to the concept of gauging a subsystem symmetry to generate fracton topological order [120, 177, 178, 179, 180, 181]. The spinon bound state condensation approach can be generalized to build Ising CSLs on a variety of lattices constructed from intersecting chains. While the octochlore lattice is the next-simplest after the pyrochlore, it will be very interesting to explore Ising systems on other corner-sharing-cluster lattices with more spins per cluster, giving rise to additional multipole moments, more spin liquids, and more exotic phases intermediate between spin liquids and ordered phases.

VIII.4 Extensions of the Octochlore Ising Model

One obvious path forward is to explore extensions of the minimal Ising model we have studied here with the addition of the inter-octahedra J2​bJ_{2b} interaction, and to develop an irrep analysis for system with interaction between the corner-sharing clusters. Studying the extended J1J_{1}-J2​aJ_{2a}-J2​bJ_{2b} phase diagram of the Ising model will be relevant for modeling the ground states of the rare earth anti-perovskites Ce3​NIn\text{Ce}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{NIn} [62] and Ho3​InC\text{Ho}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{3}}}\text{InC} [65]. Furthermore, we expect interesting frustrated magnetism physics to occur along the J1J_{1}-J2​bJ_{2b} line—whereas the pure-J2​aJ_{2a} model leads to decoupled 1D chains, the pure-J2​bJ_{2b} model leads to decoupled 2D planar Ising models, which are coupled together by the J1J_{1} interaction, likely leading to some analog of the frustrated chains phase. Moreover, we expect an additional exotic classical spin liquid on the J1J_{1}-J2​bJ_{2b} line, such as a spin vorticity model which realizes a 2-form U(1) spin liquid whose excitations are strings rather than particles [55]. In particular, it will be interesting to examine how this spin liquid arises from a mechanism similar to the spinon bound state condensation discussed in Section IV.2.

VIII.5 Anisotropic Octochlore Spin Hamiltonians

Another promising direction is to investigate the three-component classical spin model on this lattice, retaining the SxS^{x} and SyS^{y} spin components and incorporating all symmetry-allowed anisotropic interactions. Such an approach would parallel the corresponding program on the pyrochlore lattice, which has provided impetus for the study of exotic phases in strongly correlated frustrated spin systems [182, 183, 3]. The phase diagram of the three-component bilinear spin model on the pyrochlore lattice including all symmetry-allowed anisotropic interactions has been fully mapped in the classical limit using the irreducible multipole approach [41, 30], and found to harbor a variety of classical spin liquids [35, 42, 41, 39, 43, 40, 38, 3] and other frustrated behaviors including spin nematicity [56, 35, 43, 36]. There is little doubt that the analogous anisotropic model on the octochlore lattice will harbor analogous phases and spin liquids with quite likely even more complex behaviors. Indeed, as have shown in this work, the octahedral unit exhibits richer physics than the tetrahedral unit owing to its increased number of spins and corresponding additional competing irreducible multipole modes. A concrete problem of experimental relevance to the rare-earth fluoride insulating compounds discussed in Section VII is to determine the types of symmetry-allowed crystal field doublets which occur in this family of compounds; in the pyrochlore there exist three distinct types of doublets—pseudospin-1/2, non-Kramers, and dipolar-octupolar [183]—each with their own spin Hamiltonian dictating their low-temperature physics [3, 17].

VIII.6 U(1) X-Cube Quantum Spin Liquid

The full anisotropic model including all spin components will contain terms such as Si+​Sj−S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}, Si+​Sj+S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{+}, and Siz​Si+S_{i}^{z}S_{i}^{+}, where S±=Sx±i​Sy\smash{\cramped{S^{\pm}=S^{x}\pm iS^{y}}} act to flip spins in the SzS^{z} basis. If these are added perturbatively to the classical SzS^{z} model studied in this work, they may be viewed as generating quantum dynamics (kinetic energy) for the various quasiparticle excitations which appear throughout the phase diagram. It is of particular interest to explore the physics of the classical X-cube cage-net CSL studied in Section V when perturbed by such terms, which perturbatively generate ring exchange—quantum processes which tunnel between classical ground states, promoting a classical spin liquid to a quantum spin liquid [54]. For the X-cube CSL, it is straightforward to write down a quantum ring exchange term which performs the cage-net move shown in Fig. 6(a). The resulting effective Hamiltonian will map to a U(1) lattice gauge theory [54, 55], specifically a spin-1/2 quantum link model [184] realization of the U(1) X-cube lattice gauge theory [140]. This should give rise to a quantum spin liquid hosting a photon-like excitation which is gapless along 1D lines in reciprocal space [140], arising from the nodal line in the band structure. Quantum fluctuations will likely also give rise to rich sub-dimensional dynamics in both the frustrated chains and spin nematic phases, which will be of great interest to explore.

VIII.7 Outlook

Altogether, our work lays the groundwork for the exploration of highly frustrated 3D Ising systems beyond the pyrochlore lattice, advancing the theoretical methods for studying these systems and paving the road towards new experimentally-accessible materials for studying 3D frustrated magnetism. On the theoretical front, we have extended techniques used in the continuous-spin analysis of frustrated magnets to the study of Ising systems, providing a clean demonstration of the usefulness and physical meaning of the multipolar irreps in the characterization of frustrated phases. We uncovered a classical fracton CSL that broadens the spin ice paradigm, together with a striking set of frustrated phases intermediate between spin liquids and conventional long-range order. On the experimental front, our work establishes that Ising-like rare-earth magnets in corner-sharing geometries beyond the pyrochlore’s tetrahedra are a highly promising target for further study. We hope our work will inspire the further development and fruitful investigation of both rare-earth anti-perovskite and octochlore fluoride compounds, and spur on the search for other magnetic rare-earth octochlore materials which, one may enthusiastically hope, could constitute a next-generation platform for 3D frustrated magnets.

Appendix A Lattice Conventions

The octochlore lattice is the line graph of the cubic lattice, meaning that each octochlore site sits at the midpoint of a cubic lattice edge [7]. Since there are three edges per cubic lattice unit cell, it is natural to use a 3-site primitive unit cell. On the other hand, it is convenient to use a 6-site unit cell which contains all six sites of a single octahedron, with an fcc lattice. For the purpose of Monte Carlo simulations with periodic boundaries, on the other hand, it is convenient to use a a larger 24-site unit cell with a cubic space lattice with enlarged spacing. Denoting the Cartesian cubic axis unit vectors 𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}}, 𝒚^\hat{\bm{y}}, 𝒛^\hat{\bm{z}}, and general vectors by

and −[a​b​c]≡[a¯​b¯​c¯]-[abc]\equiv[\bar{a}\bar{b}\bar{c}], these unit cells have translation vectors
