Appendix B Irreducible Representations and Multipoles

In Section II, we described the phase diagram of the Hamiltonian Eq. 1 using irreducible representations of the point group, illustrated in Fig. 1(b-d); we expand further on this here.

The use of irreps to study the phase diagram of corner-sharing clusters has seen extensive use in studying nearest-neighbor anisotropic Heisenberg models on the pyrochlore lattice [30, 45, 39, 41, 42, 3]. In particular, spin liquids occur when multiple irreps are tuned to be degenerate in the ground state [45, 39, 41, 42, 3]. Previous works have not explored the application of these irreps for Ising models. The octochlore lattice is an excellent platform for its application to Ising models due to having two inequivalent interactions within the octahedra and thus the resulting rich phase diagram studied in the main text. The octochlore Hamiltonian we study decomposes into a sum over octahedra

H=12​∑o∑⟨i​j⟩∈oSiz​𝒥i​j​Sjz,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathrm{o}}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\in\mathrm{o}}S_{i}^{z}\mathcal{J}_{ij}S_{j}^{z}, (39)

where the single-octahedron interaction matrix is given using the sublattice ordering convention in Eq. 33 by

Ji​j=(0J1J1J2​aJ1J1J10J1J1J2​aJ1J1J10J1J1J2​aJ2​aJ1J10J1J1J1J2​aJ1J10J1J1J1J2​aJ1J10).J_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}0&J_{1}&J_{1}&J_{2a}&J_{1}&J_{1}\\ J_{1}&0&J_{1}&J_{1}&J_{2a}&J_{1}\\ J_{1}&J_{1}&0&J_{1}&J_{1}&J_{2a}\\ J_{2a}&J_{1}&J_{1}&0&J_{1}&J_{1}\\ J_{1}&J_{2a}&J_{1}&J_{1}&0&J_{1}\\ J_{1}&J_{1}&J_{2a}&J_{1}&J_{1}&0\\ \end{pmatrix}. (40)

The symmetries of the octahedron are described by the group OhO_{h}, which acts on the six Ising spins by permutations of the sublattice position. This 6-dimensional representation PP can be decomposed into irreducible representations, where the number of copies of irrep Γ\Gamma is given by the formula [185]

nΓ=dΓ|Oh|​∑g∈OhχΓ​(g)∗​Tr⁡[P⁡(g)],n_{\Gamma}=\frac{d_{\Gamma}}{|O_{h}|}\sum_{g\in O_{h}}\chi_{\Gamma}(g)^{*}\Tr[P(g)], (41)

where gg are the group elements of OhO_{h}, |Oh|=48|O_{h}|=48, χΓ​(g)\chi_{\Gamma}(g) is the character (trace) of gg in irrep Γ\Gamma, and dΓd_{\Gamma} is the dimension of the irrep. This results in the decomposition P=A1​u⊕Eu⊕T1​g{P=A_{1u}\oplus E_{u}\oplus T_{1g}}. Since Eq. 40 commutes with all of the P⁡(g)P(g) permutation matrices, its eigenvalues are labeled by Γ\Gamma and are each dΓd_{\Gamma} degenerate. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors are given in Table 2, which are used to write the Hamiltonian in the form of Eq. 5.

These irreps correspond to cluster multipole moments [105] of the octahedral spin configuration, as defined in Eq. 3 using the 6-site basis. To see this, let 𝒅i=(1/2)​g​μB​Siz​𝒛^i\cramped{\bm{d}_{i}=(1/2)g\mu_{\text{B}}S_{i}^{z}\hat{\bm{z}}_{i}} denote the local dipole moment vector. The three-dimensional T1​gT_{1g} irrep describes the net dipole moment of an octahedron,

doα=∑i∈odiα∝∑i∈oSiz​z^iα.d^{\alpha}_{\mathrm{o}}=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{o}}d_{i}^{\alpha}\propto\sum_{i\in\mathrm{o}}S_{i}^{z}\hat{z}_{i}^{\alpha}. (42)

The other two irreps are contained in the rank-2 moment tensor,

ℳoα​β=∑i∈o(riα−roα)​diβ,\mathcal{M}^{\alpha\beta}_{\mathrm{o}}=\sum_{i\in{\mathrm{o}}}(r_{i}^{\alpha}-r_{\mathrm{o}}^{\alpha})\,d_{i}^{\beta}, (43)

where 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} is the position of site ii and 𝒓o\bm{r}_{\mathrm{o}} is the position of the center of the octahedron. The trace of this tensor gives the A1​uA_{1u} irrep order parameter,

Tr⁡[ℳo]=∑i∈o𝒛^i⋅𝒅i∝∑i∈oSiz,\Tr[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{o}}]=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{o}}\hat{\bm{z}}_{i}\cdot\bm{d}_{i}\propto\sum_{i\in{\mathrm{o}}}S_{i}^{z}, (44)

which may be interpreted as the “monopole moment” of the octahedron since it is a scalar maximized in the all-in or all-out configurations. Note that ℳ\mathcal{M} has zero off-diagonal components because the 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} point along the cubic axes, so z^iα​z^iβ=0\smash{\hat{z}_{i}^{\alpha}\hat{z}_{i}^{\beta}=0} if α≠β\alpha\neq\beta. Subtracting its trace, we obtain the quadrupole moment tensor,

𝒬oα​β=ℳoα​β−13​Tr⁡[ℳo]​δα​β∝∑i∈oSiz​(z^iα​z^iβ−13​δα​β).\mathcal{Q}^{\alpha\beta}_{\mathrm{o}}=\mathcal{M}^{\alpha\beta}_{\mathrm{o}}-\frac{1}{3}\Tr[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{o}}]\delta^{\alpha\beta}\propto\sum_{i\in\mathrm{o}}S_{i}^{z}\left(\hat{z}_{i}^{\alpha}\hat{z}_{i}^{\beta}-\frac{1}{3}\delta_{\alpha\beta}\right). (45)

The off-diagonal elements of this tensor are zero, leaving only two independent degrees of freedom of the trace-free diagonal, forming the two-component EuE_{u} irrep. They correspond to the 3​z2−r23z^{2}-r^{2} and x2−y2x^{2}-y^{2} components of the quadrupole tensor, the first and second EuE_{u} eigenvectors listed in Table 2, respectively. The expressions in Eq. 3 are dimensionless versions of these multipole moments.

A few comments on the multipoles defined in Eq. 3 are in order. The alternating signs (−1)o(-1)^{\mathrm{o}} ensure that the ungerade irrep monopole and quadrupole moments receive positive contributions from “out” spins and negative contributions from “in” spins. Note, however, that the gerade irrep dipole moment 𝑫o\bm{D}_{\mathrm{o}} points in the opposite direction of the net magnetic moment for 𝖡\mathsf{B}-sublattice octahedra. While we could omit the sign in the definition of 𝑫o\bm{D}_{\mathrm{o}} so that it always points in the direction of the physical dipole moment, including the sign allows for a more unified treatment of the phase diagram because the staggered moment is locally conserved by Néel domain walls. In particular, the A1​u⊕EuA_{1u}\oplus E_{u} decoupled AFM chains point can be treated in a parallel manner to the A1​u⊕T1​gA_{1u}\oplus T_{1g} X-cube CSL and the Eu⊕T1​gE_{u}\oplus T_{1g} spin ice CSL, whose excitations carry locally conserved EuE_{u} quadrupole and A1​uA_{1u} monopole charge, respectively. Lastly, a terminological point—we have labeled ϕo\phi_{\mathrm{o}} the monopole moment, which agrees with the notion that the “hedgehog”-like all-out configuration in Fig. 1(a) looks like a positively charged magnetic monopole, and indeed behaves like one in the spin ice spin liquid, especially when long-range dipole-dipole interactions are included [29, 9]. In terms of the physical magnetic field produced by the dipole moments, however, this configuration sources a hexadecapolar field.

1. Irrep Decomposition of Spin Configurations

An octahedron, decorated with Ising spins, has 26=642^{6}=64 different configurations. These split into (32×2)(32\times 2) states and their time-reversal partners and can be further classified according to their total spin and the symmetry group of the octahedron. We collect the spin configurations in Table 3, showing their decomposition into the irreducible representations A1​uA_{1u} (monopole), EuE_{u} (quadrupole), and T1​gT_{1g} (dipole).

Appendix C Interaction Matrices and Structure Factors

In this Appendix we provide the interaction matrices from which the band structures are computed, summarize the self-consistent Gaussian approximation which is used to compute correlation functions, and discuss the structure factors shown in Fig. 7.

1. Interaction Matrices

Using the 6-site unit cell, the bilinear Hamiltonian Eq. 1 can be written in terms of adjacency matrices of the octochlore lattice,

H\displaystyle H =J12​∑i​jSiz​Ai​j(1)​Sjz+J2​a2​∑i​jSiz​Ai​j(2​a)​Sjz\displaystyle=\frac{J_{1}}{2}\sum_{ij}S_{i}^{z}A^{(1)}_{ij}S_{j}^{z}+\frac{J_{2a}}{2}\sum_{ij}S_{i}^{z}A^{(2a)}_{ij}S_{j}^{z}
≡12​∑i​jSiz​[J1​Ai​j(1)+J2​a​Ai​j(2​a)]⏟𝒥i​j​Sjz,\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}S_{i}^{z}\underbrace{[J_{1}A^{(1)}_{ij}+J_{2a}A^{(2a)}_{ij}]}_{\mathcal{J}_{ij}}S_{j}^{z}, (46)

where Ai​j(n)=1\cramped{A^{(n)}_{ij}=1} if sites ii and jj are nn’th-nearest-neighbors, and 00 otherwise, and the factors of 1/21/2 removes the double counting. We refer to the matrix 𝒥i​j\mathcal{J}_{ij} as the interaction matrix. Here, the Ising variables, normalized as Siz=±1\cramped{S_{i}^{z}=\pm 1}, refer to a dipole oriented along the local 𝒛^i\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} axis defined in Eq. 32 and Eq. 33. This means that J2​a>0\cramped{J_{2a}>0} energetically prefers ferromagnetic alignment of the physical dipoles along the 1D chains coupled by the second neighbor interaction.

In the 3-site unit cell, the Fourier transformed adjacency matrices have the form

Aμ​ν(1)​(𝒒)\displaystyle A^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q}) =4​(0sx​sysx​szsx​sy0sy​szsx​szsy​sz0),\displaystyle=4\begin{pmatrix}0&s_{x}s_{y}&s_{x}s_{z}\\[1.0pt] s_{x}s_{y}&0&s_{y}s_{z}\\[1.0pt] s_{x}s_{z}&s_{y}s_{z}&0\end{pmatrix},
Aμ​ν(2​a)​(𝒒)\displaystyle A^{(2a)}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q}) =−2​(cx​x+000cy​y+000cz​z+),\displaystyle=-2\begin{pmatrix}c_{xx}^{+}&0&0\\[1.0pt] 0&c_{yy}^{+}&0\\[1.0pt] 0&0&c_{zz}^{+}\end{pmatrix}, (47)

where μ,ν\mu,\nu are sublattice indices and we define

sα≡sin⁡(qα4)andcα​β±≡cos⁡(qα±qβ4).s_{\alpha}\equiv\sin\left(\frac{q_{\alpha}}{4}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad c_{\alpha\beta}^{\pm}\equiv\cos\left(\frac{q_{\alpha}\pm q_{\beta}}{4}\right). (48)

The negative sign in front of Aμ​ν(2​a)​(𝒒)A_{\mu\nu}^{(2a)}(\bm{q}) is included in Eq. 47 because in the unit cell of 3-sites, a positive J2​aJ_{2a} prefers the antiferromagnetic alignment of the chains. With this choice, Eq. 46 is the same Hamiltonian for either basis choice. In the 6-site unit cell the adjacency matrices are given by

Aμ​ν(1)​(𝒒)=2​(0cx​y−cx​z−0cx​y+cx​z+cx​y−0cy​z−cx​y+0cy​z+cx​z−cy​z−0cx​z+cy​z+00cx​y+cx​z+0cx​y−cx​z−cx​y+0cy​z+cx​y−0cy​z−cx​z+cy​z+0cx​z−cy​z−0),A^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q})=2\begin{pmatrix}0&c_{xy}^{-}&c_{xz}^{-}&0&c_{xy}^{+}&c_{xz}^{+}\\[1.0pt] c_{xy}^{-}&0&c_{yz}^{-}&c_{xy}^{+}&0&c_{yz}^{+}\\[1.0pt] c_{xz}^{-}&c_{yz}^{-}&0&c_{xz}^{+}&c_{yz}^{+}&0\\[1.0pt] 0&c_{xy}^{+}&c_{xz}^{+}&0&c_{xy}^{-}&c_{xz}^{-}\\[1.0pt] c_{xy}^{+}&0&c_{yz}^{+}&c_{xy}^{-}&0&c_{yz}^{-}\\[1.0pt] c_{xz}^{+}&c_{yz}^{+}&0&c_{xz}^{-}&c_{yz}^{-}&0\end{pmatrix}, (49)
Aμ​ν(2​a)​(𝒒)=2​(000cx​x+000000cy​y+000000cz​z+cx​x+000000cy​y+000000cz​z+000).A^{(2a)}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q})=2\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&c_{xx}^{+}&0&0\\ 0&0&0&0&c_{yy}^{+}&0\\ 0&0&0&0&0&c_{zz}^{+}\\ c_{xx}^{+}&0&0&0&0&0\\ 0&c_{yy}^{+}&0&0&0&0\\ 0&0&c_{zz}^{+}&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}. (50)

For the purpose of counting the zero-energy locus of the interaction matrix (after shifting its minimum eigenvalue to zero), as reported in the last column of Table 1, one should always use the primitive 3-site unit cell, since the bands of the enlarged conventional unit cells yields are folded versions of the primitive bands.

2. Self-Consistent Gaussian Approximation

The self-consistent Gaussian approximation (SCGA) [186] is a simple soft-spin approximation which works well for computing correlation functions so long as the system remains paramagnetic, in particular for spin liquids. This method replaces the hard spin length constraint |Siz|=1|S_{i}^{z}|=1 with a soft one, meaning that the SizS_{i}^{z} are treated as real-valued variables which vary continuously, with the spin length enforced on average. Given a bilinear spin Hamiltonian

H=12​∑i​jSiz​𝒥i​j​Sjz,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}S_{i}^{z}\mathcal{J}_{ij}S_{j}^{z}, (51)

we add a term which energetically regulates the spin length from growing arbitrarily large,

HSCGA=H+12​∑iλi​T​(Siz)2,H_{\text{SCGA}}=H+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}T(S_{i}^{z})^{2}, (52)

where the λi\lambda_{i} are to be determined self-consistently by the requirement that ⟨|Siz|2⟩λ,T=1\langle|S_{i}^{z}|^{2}\rangle_{\lambda,T}=1 ∀i\forall i, and where the angle brackets denote a thermal expectation value at fixed λ\lambda and temperature TT. The Hamiltonian simplifies to

β​HSCGA=12​∑i​jSiz​(Λi​j+β​𝒥i​j)​Sjz\beta H_{\text{SCGA}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}S_{i}^{z}(\Lambda_{ij}+\beta\mathcal{J}_{ij})S_{j}^{z} (53)

where β=1/T\cramped{\beta=1/T} is inverse temperature, and Λi​j=λi​δi​j\cramped{\Lambda_{ij}=\lambda_{i}\delta_{ij}} with δ\delta the Kronecker delta. The partition function is then a simple multi-variate Gaussian, and one can directly read off the correlation functions

𝒢​({λi})i​j=⟨Siz​Sjz⟩=[Λ+β​𝒥]i​j−1,\mathscr{G}(\{\lambda_{i}\})_{ij}=\langle S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\rangle=[\Lambda+\beta\mathcal{J}]^{-1}_{ij}, (54)

and the self-consistency condition reads 𝒢i​i=1\mathcal{G}_{ii}=1 for all ii. For a system in which every site ii is equivalent by symmetry, the problem simplifies since all λi=λ\lambda_{i}=\lambda. The self-consistency condition can then be simplified to an average over all sites,

1Nsites​Tr⁡[𝒢⁡(λ)]=1.\frac{1}{N_{\text{sites}}}\Tr[\mathscr{G}(\lambda)]=1. (55)

In practice this is solved by Fourier transformation to block-diagonalize 𝒥\mathcal{J}, then numerically solving the self-consistency equation. In this work we utilize the SCGA to compute the structure factors shown in Fig. 7(b,c), which show excellent agreement with the Monte Carlo calculations.

3. Structure Factors and Neutron Scattering

The full two-point correlation function 𝒢i​j=⟨Siz​Sjz⟩\mathscr{G}_{ij}=\langle S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}\rangle can be Fourier transformed as

𝒢μ​ν​(𝒒)=⟨Sμz​(−𝒒)​Sνz​(𝒒)⟩,\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q})=\langle S^{z}_{\mu}(-\bm{q})S^{z}_{\nu}(\bm{q})\rangle, (56)

using Eq. 36. Due to the sublattice structure, this quantity is a tensor at each wavevector 𝒒\bm{q}, which contains the full information about the spin correlations. Structure factors are a contraction of this tensor with a form factor to obtain one scalar value per 𝒒\bm{q}. The simplest is the spin structure factor, defined as

S⁡(𝒒)=∑μ​ν𝒢μ​ν​(𝒒).S(\bm{q})=\sum_{\mu\nu}\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q}). (57)

Note that this structure factor depends on the choice of unit cell as it is defined in terms of the gauge-dependent quantities SizS_{i}^{z}. Furthermore, because the form factor is 𝒒\bm{q}-independent, this structure factor may not fully reflect the angular dependence of the correlation tensor. This is the case for the X-cube fracton spin liquid discussed in Section V, which has nodal line singularities with quadrupolar angular dependence—the spin structure factor only exposes two-fold pinch points at the zone centers and exhibits smooth behavior along the nodal lines.

Exposing the angular dependence requires the introduction of a 𝒒\bm{q}-dependent form factor. Such a form factor appears naturally in neutron scattering experiments—neutrons are scattered by the divergence-free magnetic field produced by the local Ising magnetic moments 𝒅i∝Si​𝒛^i\bm{d}_{i}\propto S_{i}\hat{\bm{z}}_{i} of the ions in the lattice [152]. We define the dimensionless moment-moment correlation tensor,

𝒢μ​να​β​(𝒒)=⟨d^μα​(−𝒒)​d^νβ​(𝒒)⟩≡z^μα​z^νβ​𝒢μ​ν​(𝒒),\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q})=\langle\hat{d}_{\mu}^{\alpha}(-\bm{q})\hat{d}_{\nu}^{\beta}(\bm{q})\rangle\equiv\hat{z}_{\mu}^{\alpha}\hat{z}_{\nu}^{\beta}\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}(\bm{q}), (58)

which is independent of the gauge choices of quantization axes. For unpolarized neutrons, the scattering cross section is proportional to

Sunp​(𝒒)=∑μ,ν∑α,β(δα​β−q^α​q^β)​𝒢μ​να​β​(𝒒),S_{\text{unp}}(\bm{q})=\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\left(\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\hat{q}^{\alpha}\hat{q}^{\beta}\right)\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q}), (59)

where the projector arises because the magnetic field is divergence-free, so neutrons do not “see” the longitudinal (along 𝒒^\hat{\bm{q}}) component of the correlations. Polarization analysis further refines this cross-section into two channels, denoted spin-flip (SF) and non-spin-flip (NSF), referring to filtering the scattered neutrons according to whether they are flipped or not in the scattering process [152]. We consider incident neutrons initially polarized in the direction 𝒛^s\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}. For each scattering wavevector 𝒒\bm{q} such that 𝒒⟂𝒛^s\bm{q}\perp\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}, we define a local orthonormal frame {𝒙^s,𝒚^s,𝒛^s}\{\hat{\bm{x}}_{s},\hat{\bm{y}}_{s},\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}\}, where 𝒙^s=𝒒^\hat{\bm{x}}_{s}=\hat{\bm{q}} and 𝒚^s=𝒛^s×𝒙^s\hat{\bm{y}}_{s}=\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}\times\hat{\bm{x}}_{s} [21, 150]. The SF and NSF cross-sections are then proportional to the following structure factors,

SSF​(𝒒)\displaystyle S_{\textrm{SF}}(\bm{q}) =∑μ,ν∑α,βy^αsy^βs𝒢μ​να​β(𝒒)(𝒒⟂𝒛^s),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\hat{y}^{\alpha}_{s}\hat{y}^{\beta}_{s}\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q})\quad(\bm{q}\perp\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}), (60)
SNSF​(𝒒)\displaystyle S_{\textrm{NSF}}(\bm{q}) =∑μ,ν∑α,βz^αsz^βs𝒢μ​να​β(𝒒)(𝒒⟂𝒛^s),\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu,\nu}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\hat{z}^{\alpha}_{s}\hat{z}^{\beta}_{s}\mathscr{G}_{\mu\nu}^{\alpha\beta}(\bm{q})\quad(\bm{q}\perp\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}),

which satisfy

Sunp​(𝒒)=SSF​(𝒒)+SNSF​(𝒒),S_{\text{unp}}(\bm{q})=S_{\text{SF}}(\bm{q})+S_{\text{NSF}}(\bm{q}), (61)

because the vectors 𝒙^s\hat{\bm{x}}_{s}, 𝒚^s\hat{\bm{y}}_{s}, 𝒛^s\hat{\bm{z}}_{s} form an orthonormal basis at each 𝒒⟂𝒛^s\bm{q}\perp\hat{\bm{z}}_{s}.

Appendix D Specific Heat of 1D Chains

In Fig. 10(a), we fit the low-temperature specific heat of the spin nematic phase to the exact solution for decoupled 1D chains. This solution is easily derived from the transfer matrix formulation of the partition function. For a periodic 1D chain with Hamiltonian

H1D-chain=−J~∑i=1LSizSi+1zH_{\text{1D-chain}}=-\tilde{J}\sum_{i=1}^{L}S_{i}^{z}S_{i+1}^{z} (62)

where Siz=±1S_{i}^{z}=\pm 1 and SL+1≡S1S_{L+1}\equiv S_{1}, the partition function at inverse temperature β=1/T\beta=1/T is

ZL(β)=∑{Siz=±1}∏i=1Lexp(+βJ~SizSi+1z)≡Tr[𝒯L]Z_{L}(\beta)=\sum_{\{S_{i}^{z}=\pm 1\}}\prod_{i=1}^{L}\exp(+\beta\tilde{J}S_{i}^{z}S_{i+1}^{z})\equiv\Tr[\mathcal{T}^{L}] (63)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the transfer matrix,

𝒯=(e+β​J~e−β​J~e−β​J~e+β​J~).\mathcal{T}=\begin{pmatrix}e^{+\beta\tilde{J}}&e^{-\beta\tilde{J}}\\ e^{-\beta\tilde{J}}&e^{+\beta\tilde{J}}\end{pmatrix}. (64)

The heat capacity for the 1D chain is then

CV(1D,L)​(T)=∂⟨H⟩∂T=∂∂T​(−∂∂β​ln⁡ZL).C_{V}^{(\text{1D},L)}(T)=\frac{\partial\langle H\rangle}{\partial T}=\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(-\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\,\ln Z_{L}\right). (65)

In the thermodynamic limit L→∞L\to\infty, the partition function is approximated by the largest eigenvalue of the transfer matrix, so

ZL→∞∝cosh⁡(β​J~)L.Z_{L\to\infty}\propto\cosh(\beta\tilde{J})^{L}. (66)

From this we obtain the exact expression for the specific heat in the thermodynamic limit

CV(1D)/L→L→∞(β​J~)2​sech2​(β​J~)C_{V}^{\text{(1D)}}/L\,\xrightarrow{L\to\infty}\,(\beta\tilde{J})^{2}\mathrm{sech}^{2}(\beta\tilde{J}) (67)

which is precisely the form of a Schottky anomaly for a 2-level system with gap 2​J~2\tilde{J}, i.e. a smooth crossover associated to thermal depopulation of domain walls (spinons) with energy 2​J~2\tilde{J}.

We show in Fig. 10(a) a comparison of the low-temperature heat capacity per spin (with 3​L33L^{3} total spins) of the 3D system to that of L2L^{2} decoupled length-LL 1D chains with J~=J2​a\tilde{J}=J_{2a},

CV(3D)​(T)3​L3≈L2​CV(1D,L)​(T)3​L3.\frac{C_{V}^{(\text{3D})}(T)}{3L^{3}}\approx\frac{L^{2}C_{V}^{(\text{1D},L)}(T)}{3L^{3}}. (68)

At the point in the phase diagram where the data in Fig. 10(a) is taken, with 2​J1=−J2​a>02J_{1}=-J_{2a}>0, we have J2​a=2​J/5J_{2a}=2J/\sqrt{5}, with JJ defined in Eq. 2 and used in the temperature scale of Fig. 10(a).

Appendix E Cluster Algorithm for Fracton CSL

Otsuka developed a highly efficient cluster algorithm for the simulation of nearest-neighbor pyrochlore spin ice [77], which can be straightforwardly adapted for octochlore spin ice [58]. Here we explain how the algorithm works, how it is adapted to work for octochlore spin ices, and how it is amended for the X-cube fracton spin studied in Section V.

1. Graph Decomposition Algorithm

The algorithm works by a graph decomposition of the partition function, see Ref. [77] for details. The result is a decomposition of any spin configuration into clusters of spins connected by graphs, each of which may be flipped independently with 50%\% probability. Each octahedron is assigned one of a number of graphs GG such that the Boltzmann weight for a spin configuration SS can be expanded as a sum over graphs,

exp⁡[−β⁡(E⁡([S])−ϵ0)]≡w⁡([S])=∑GΔS,G​w​([G]).\exp[-\beta(E([S])-\epsilon_{0})]\equiv w([S])=\sum_{G}\Delta_{S,G}\,w([G]). (69)

Here, [S][S] denotes an equivalence class of single-octahedron spin configurations that are related by a point group transformation, and [G][G] denotes an equivalence class of graphs. For convenience, we subtract the single-octahedron ground state energy ϵ0\epsilon_{0}, so that the minimum-energy configurations have w⁡([S])=1w([S])=1. The w⁡([G])w([G]) are the graph weights, and the ΔS,G\Delta_{S,G} are the compatibility coefficients, defined as

ΔS,G={1if G is compatible with S,0otherwise.\Delta_{S,G}=\begin{cases}1&\quad\text{if $G$ is compatible with $S$,}\\ 0&\quad\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (70)

Each graph equivalence class [G][G] must contain all symmetry-equivalent graphs, but may contain multiple graphs which are not related by symmetry. To obtain the graph weights, Eq. 69 is rewritten as

w⁡([S])=∑[G]Γ[S],[G]​w​([G]),w([S])=\sum_{[G]}\Gamma_{[S],[G]}\,w([G]), (71)

where we have defined the reduced compatibility matrix

Γ[S],[G]=∑G∈[G]ΔS,G,\Gamma_{[S],[G]}=\sum_{G\in[G]}\Delta_{S,G}, (72)

which counts how many graphs in a given class [G][G] are compatible with a given spin configuration SS. This quantity depends only on the symmetry class [S][S] since each [G][G] contains all symmetry-equivalent graphs. In this form, we can see that solving for w⁡([G])w([G]) can be done by inverting the matrix Γ[S],[G]\Gamma_{[S],[G]}, assuming that the number of spin classes [S][S] is the same as the number of graph classes [G][G],

w⁡([G])=∑[S]Γ[G],[S]−1​w​([S]).w([G])=\sum_{[S]}\Gamma^{-1}_{[G],[S]}\,w([S]). (73)

The probabilities for assigning graph GG to spin configuration SS is then given by [77]

p⁡(G|S)=ΔS,G​w​([G])/w⁡([S]).p(G|S)=\Delta_{S,G}\,w([G])/w([S]). (74)

Note that ∑Gp⁡(G|S)=1\sum_{G}p(G|S)=1 using Eq. 71, i.e. the total probability of assigning a graph to a spin configuration is unity. The algorithm works by fixing a spin configuration, applying a random graph GG to every octahedron with probability given by Eq. 74, identifying the resulting clusters obtained by gluing graphs on neighboring octahedra, and flipping each cluster with 50%\% probability. See Ref. [77] for further details. It is useful to define the total probability of assigning any graph in class [G][G] to a spin configuration SS,

p⁡([G]|[S])=∑G∈[G]p⁡(G|S)=Γ[S],[G]​w⁡([G])w⁡([S]),p([G]|[S])=\sum_{G\in[G]}p(G|S)\,=\,\Gamma_{[S],[G]}\frac{w([G])}{w([S])}, (75)

which only depends on the symmetry class [S][S] since we sum over all symmetry-equivalent graphs GG. In practice, for each octahedron we pick a graph class according to p⁡([G]|[S])p([G]|[S]) and then pick one of the compatible G∈[G]G\in[G] with equal probability.

2. Cluster Algorithm for Spin Ice CSL

The graph types [G][G] must be chosen in a way that is compatible with the ground state constraints. In the case of spin ice, the ground state satisfies a zero-divergence constraint and is therefore a string condensate (where a string connects an in-spin to an out-spin), with no restriction on the geometry of the strings. Thus the graphs should be chosen to pair up in with out spins on each octahedron and their weights w⁡([G])w([G]) depend only on the number of “loose ends” of the strings, see Ref. [58] for further details.

3. Cluster Algorithm for X-cube CSL

At the X-cube point, J2​a=−2​J1>0J_{2a}=-2J_{1}>0, we distinguish the six symmetry-classes of spin configurations and their energies in Fig. 13(a). Defining

z=exp⁡(−2​β​J2​a),z=\exp(-2\beta J_{2a}), (76)

the Boltzmann weights are

w⁡([S]1)\displaystyle w([S]_{1}) =1,w([S]3)=z,w([S]5)=z3,\displaystyle=1,\quad w([S]_{3})=z,\quad w([S]_{5})=z^{3}, (77)
w⁡([S]2)\displaystyle w([S]_{2}) =1,w([S]4)=z,w([S]6)=z4.\displaystyle=1,\quad w([S]_{4})=z,\quad w([S]_{6})=z^{4}.

Whereas spin ice realizes a string-net liquid, according to our discussion in Section V.1, the X-cube CSL realizes a cage-net liquid where the flippable motifs are cages like the ones shown in Fig. 6(a,b). Accordingly, we choose graphs as shown in Fig. 13(b), which contain either straight segments ([G]1[G]_{1} through [G]4[G]_{4}) or corners ([G]5[G]_{5} and [G]6[G]_{6}). Below each graph, we give the number of symmetry-equivalent graphs in the equivalence class. Gluing such graphs together produces cage nets like those shown in Fig. 6(a,b). Graphs [G]1[G]_{1}, [G]2[G]_{2}, [G]3[G]_{3}, and [G]5[G]_{5} have disconnected spins, indicated in orange, which produce cage nets with open ends. The compatibility coefficients ΔS,G\Delta_{S,G} depend only on the graph class, and are given by

ΔS,G∈[G]n={{1​ if S1z=−S2z0​ otherwisen=2,3,4,{1​ if S1z=S2z=S3z0​ otherwisen=5,6,1n=1,\Delta_{S,{G\in[G]_{n}}}=\begin{cases}\begin{array}[]{ll}\begin{cases}1\text{ if $S_{1}^{z}=-S_{2}^{z}$}\\ 0\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}&n=2,3,4,\\[2.15277pt] \begin{cases}1\text{ if $S_{1}^{z}=S_{2}^{z}=S_{3}^{z}$}\\ 0\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}&n=5,6,\\[2.15277pt] \qquad\quad 1&n=1,\end{array}\end{cases} (78)

where the SizS_{i}^{z} are given in the 6-site basis, and refer only to spins which are connected by the graph. In words: the first case refers to the straight segment graphs n=2,3,4n=2,3,4. These graphs can only connect pairs of spins with one spin “in” and the other “out”. The second case refers to the corner graphs n=5,6n=5,6, and these graphs can only connect a trio of spins with all three spins “in” or all three spins “out”. The third case refers to the free graph n=1n=1, which is compatible with any spin configuration. The reduced compatibility matrix Γ[S],[G]\Gamma_{[S],[G]} is given by

Γ[S],[G]=([G]1[G]2[G]3[G]4[G]5[G]6[S]1133121[S]2100084[S]3121020[S]4110040[S]5110000[S]6100000).\Gamma_{[S],[G]}=\left({\begin{array}[]{c|cccccc}&[G]_{1}&[G]_{2}&[G]_{3}&[G]_{4}&[G]_{5}&[G]_{6}\\[2.0pt] \hline\cr\\[-8.0pt] {[S]}_{1}&1&3&3&1&2&1\\[6.0pt] {[S]}_{2}&1&0&0&0&8&4\\[6.0pt] {[S]}_{3}&1&2&1&0&2&0\\[6.0pt] {[S]}_{4}&1&1&0&0&4&0\\[6.0pt] {[S]}_{5}&1&1&0&0&0&0\\[6.0pt] {[S]}_{6}&1&0&0&0&0&0\end{array}}\right). (79)

Inverting this matrix, we obtain the graph weights, Eq. 73,

w⁡([G]1)\displaystyle w([G]_{1}) =z4,\displaystyle=z^{4}, (80)
w⁡([G]2)\displaystyle w([G]_{2}) =z3−z4,\displaystyle=z^{3}-z^{4},
w⁡([G]3)\displaystyle w([G]_{3}) =(z−3​z3+2​z4)/2,\displaystyle=(z-3z^{3}+2z^{4})/2,
w⁡([G]4)\displaystyle w([G]_{4}) =(3−6​z+6​z3−3​z4)/4,\displaystyle=(3-6z+6z^{3}-3z^{4})/4,
w⁡([G]5)\displaystyle w([G]_{5}) =(z−z3)/4,\displaystyle=(z-z^{3})/4,
w⁡([G]6)\displaystyle w([G]_{6}) =(1−2​z+2​z3−z4)/4.\displaystyle=(1-2z+2z^{3}-z^{4})/4.

Combining Eqs. 77, 78 and 80, we can compute the corresponding probabilities using Eq. 74. In Fig. 13(c) we plot the resulting graph class assignment probabilities, Eq. 75. Note that in a ground state consisting of only [S]1[S]_{1} and [S]2[S]_{2} octahedra, in the limit T→0T\to 0 only the fully connected graphs [G]4[G]_{4} and [G]6[G]_{6} have non-zero probabilities, and the algorithm decomposes each spin configuration into a fully packed cage net covering, analogous to the fully packed loop coverings for Coulomb liquids [115].

Appendix F Monte Carlo Simulation Details

In this appendix, we provide details of the Monte Carlo simulations. Except where noted, these are performed using the 24-site unit cell, for a system of L×L×LL\times L\times L unit cells with periodic boundaries. Some figures instead label system sizes by the equivalent 3-site linear dimension 2​L2L for consistency with the rest of the manuscript; we indicate the correspondence where relevant.

1. Thermodynamics

In our Monte Carlo simulations we compute the specific heat from the variance of the energy,

CV=1n​L3​⟨E2⟩−⟨E⟩2T2,C_{V}=\frac{1}{nL^{3}}\,\frac{\langle E^{2}\rangle-\langle E\rangle^{2}}{T^{2}}, (81)

where nn is the number of spins in the simulated unit cell (Appendix A), and uncertainties are obtained by jackknife binning. The entropy per spin is then obtained by integrating CV/TC_{V}/T [55],

S⁡(T)=S⁡(∞)−∫TTmaxCVT​𝑑T−∫Tmax∞CVT​𝑑T,S(T)=S(\infty)-\int_{T}^{T_{\max}}\frac{C_{V}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T-\int_{T_{\max}}^{\infty}\frac{C_{V}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T, (82)

where S⁡(∞)=ln⁡2S(\infty)=\ln 2 and TmaxT_{\max} is the highest temperature simulated. Since the simulations extend only up to TmaxT_{\max}, we split the integral into a numerically sampled part and a high-temperature tail. The first integral is evaluated by numerical quadrature using the CVC_{V} data in Fig. 6. For the second, we truncate the high-temperature series expansion of the specific heat,

CV≈aT2+bT3,C_{V}\approx\frac{a}{T^{2}}+\frac{b}{T^{3}}, (83)

extract aa and bb by fitting the high-temperature tail of the measured CVC_{V}, and integrate analytically,

∫Tmax∞CVT​𝑑T≈a2​Tmax2+b3​Tmax3.\int_{T_{\max}}^{\infty}\frac{C_{V}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T\approx\frac{a}{2T_{\max}^{2}}+\frac{b}{3T_{\max}^{3}}. (84)

2. Finite-Temperature Phase Diagram

In Fig. 1(f), we report critical temperatures TcT_{c} for a range of angles θ\theta on the unit-circle parametrization [Eq. 2] of the intra-octahedral phase diagram. These sweeps were performed on an L=24L=24 system using the 6-spin unit cell, with parallel tempering over 100 replicas. Each simulation comprised 10410^{4} thermalization sweeps followed by 10510^{5} measurements, with measurements taken every 10 sweeps and parallel-tempering swaps attempted every 5 sweeps. The critical temperatures TcAIAOT_{c}^{\mathrm{AIAO}} and TcuniT_{c}^{\mathrm{uni}} were identified from the location of the CVC_{V} peak. The biaxial transition produces no diverging CVC_{V} anomaly [Fig. 10(a)]; we therefore identify TcbiT_{c}^{\mathrm{bi}} as the temperature at which the two degenerate subleading eigenvalues of the quadrupole tensor split apart [Fig. 10(c)]. The resulting Tc​(θ)T_{c}(\theta) are plotted on a linear scale in Fig. 14, and reproduced on the non-linear radial scale r⁡(T/J)=1−tanh⁡[(T/10​J)1/2]r(T/J)=1-\tanh[(T/10J)^{1/2}] in Fig. 1(f).

3. Frustrated Chain Phase

In Fig. 5 we present specific-heat curves for angles θ∈{θSI,…,θXC}\theta\in\{\theta_{\mathrm{SI}},\dots,\theta_{\mathrm{XC}}\} spanning the frustrated chain phase, where θSI=45∘\theta_{\mathrm{SI}}=45^{\circ} (J1=J2​aJ_{1}=J_{2a}) and θXC\theta_{\mathrm{XC}} (J1/J2​a=−1/2J_{1}/J_{2a}=-1/2) are the two spin-liquid endpoints. At these endpoints we use the dedicated cluster algorithms of Appendix E, combined with simulated annealing to cool L=8L=8 systems from T/J=102T/J=10^{2} to T/J=10−2T/J=10^{-2} while making 10610^{6} measurements at each temperature. All other angles were simulated with an L=8L=8 system using parallel tempering with single-spin-flip updates. For angles near the spin-ice point (θ≤54∘\theta\leq 54^{\circ}), we supplement the single-spin flips with the short spin-ice loop moves of Ref. [82]. All replicas were initialized in a random ferromagnetic configuration and thermalized for 10410^{4} sweeps, with parallel-tempering swaps every 3 sweeps, before recording 5×1055\times 10^{5} measurements separated by 5 sweeps.

4. X-cube Spin Liquid

In Fig. 6(c) and Fig. 7(b,c), we present thermodynamic data for the X-cube CSL at J2​a=−2​J1>0J_{2a}=-2J_{1}>0, discussed in Section V. These use the cluster algorithm of Appendix E on L=16,20,24L=16,20,24 systems with the 24-site unit cell (Appendix A). Starting from a random configuration, we used simulated annealing to cool the system through 40 temperatures spanning Tmin<T<TmaxT_{\min}<T<T_{\max}, distributed as: linearly spaced over 0.35<T/J2​a<1.460.35<T/J_{2a}<1.46; linearly spaced over 1.5<T/J2​a<2.51.5<T/J_{2a}<2.5; and logarithmically spaced over 100.4<T/J2​a<10210^{0.4}<T/J_{2a}<10^{2}, with J2​a=J/5J_{2a}=J/\sqrt{5}. These ranges were chosen to resolve the CVC_{V} peak. At each temperature we ran 1000 independent simulations, each with 10410^{4} thermalization sweeps followed by 5000 measurements sampled every 5 sweeps, for a total of 5×1065\times 10^{6} measurements per temperature.

To evaluate the entropy [Eq. 82], we fit the high-temperature tail of the L=24L=24 specific heat for T≥50​J2​aT\geq 50J_{2a} to Eq. 83, obtaining

a=7.91±0.02,b=−31.0±0.3,a=7.91\pm 0.02,\qquad b=-31.0\pm 0.3, (85)

which gives a high-temperature entropy contribution [Eq. 84] of

∫Tmax∞CVT​𝑑T=(4.06±0.01)×10−4.\int_{T_{\max}}^{\infty}\frac{C_{V}}{T}\,\mathrm{d}T=(4.06\pm 0.01)\times 10^{-4}. (86)

The entropy S⁡(T)S(T) was then obtained by numerically integrating CV​(T)/TC_{V}(T)/T as in Eq. 82. Error bars on the full integral were estimated by resampling: we used the jackknife uncertainties on CVC_{V} to generate Nsamp=103N_{\mathrm{samp}}=10^{3} synthetic data sets, repeated the integration for each, and took the standard deviation of the resulting entropy curves as the uncertainty.

5. Spin Nematic

Figure 10 presents thermodynamic data at the point diametrically opposite the fractonic X-cube model in Fig. 1(f) labeled “Fully Packed Fractons”. Three sets of simulations underlie the figure, each targeting a different feature; all use the 24-site unit cell. Following the convention above, the L=20L=20 simulations in this section correspond to the label L=40L=40 in Figs. 10 and 11.

To expose the spontaneous breaking of rotational symmetry, we performed 250 independent simulated-annealing runs on an L=20L=20 system (40 a​bab-planes), each cooled from a random configuration at T/J=2.0T/J=2.0 to T/J=0.2T/J=0.2, equilibrating for 10410^{4} sweeps and then recording 10510^{5} measurements (every 5 sweeps) at each temperature. These runs produce the faint ensemble of eigenvalue curves in Fig. 10(c): as discussed in Section VI.3, once the a​bab-planes order [Eq. 26] the two subleading eigenvalues of QQ lock onto plateaus set by the number N∈[0,40]N\in[0,40] of planes polarized along each axis, and each seed selects a different NN. Collecting these plateau values across the 250 seeds at T/J≈0.46T/J\approx 0.46 gives the histogram on the right axis of Fig. 10(c), where the integer levels NN are marked. Although the plateau distribution is representative of the biaxial phase as a whole, at higher temperatures within the phase the eigenvalue trajectories have not yet settled cleanly onto their plateaus owing to finite-size effects; we therefore sample at T/J≈0.46T/J\approx 0.46, the low-temperature end of the biaxial phase just above the 1D-chain freezing regime, where the plateaus are most sharply resolved. The histogram is compared to the binomial distribution expected if the plane polarizations were statistically independent. The observed distribution deviates measurably from binomial, indicating that the planes are weakly correlated rather than perfectly decoupled—the sense in which the low-temperature “decoupled 1D chains” picture is a very good first approximation but not exact, as discussed further in Section VI.3. The temperature T/J≈0.46T/J\approx 0.46 also marks the high-temperature edge of the shaded region in Fig. 10, below which the correlation length of the 1D chains exceeds the system size and the chains freeze into one of their two Néel states, producing the erratic finite-size order-parameter values in Fig. 10(b,c) [cf. Fig. 11(d)]. Within this shaded region the specific heat matches the exact finite-length 1D Ising result (Appendix D), shown for the 250 seeds in the inset of Fig. 10(a); the close agreement confirms that the thermodynamics is well described by decoupled 1D chains at leading order, even though the histogram reveals residual inter-plane correlations.

To resolve the two transitions we ran parallel tempering at L=16,20,24L=16,20,24 (labels 32,40,4832,40,48), producing the scaling insets of Fig. 10(a). At Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}}, NT=64N_{T}=64 replicas were initialized randomly, thermalized for 10410^{4} sweeps, and sampled 10610^{6} times (every 5 sweeps). The biaxial transition requires more care: cooling through Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}} breaks cubic symmetry to tetragonal, so independent replicas would select different director axes and dilute a fixed-component order parameter. We therefore fix the sector by initializing all NT=64N_{T}=64 replicas (for each LL) from a single configuration annealed through Tcuni\smash{T_{c}^{\text{uni}}}, equilibrating for 10410^{4} sweeps with swaps every 3 sweeps before 10610^{6} measurements (every 10 sweeps).

The solid curves in Fig. 10(a–c) come from a single L=20L=20 parallel-tempering run over 0.1≤T/J≤2.50.1\leq T/J\leq 2.5 with NT=96N_{T}=96 replicas, initialized from an annealed ground state [as in Fig. 11], equilibrated for 10410^{4} sweeps with swaps every 3 sweeps, and sampled 10610^{6} times (every 3 sweeps). This run supplies the specific-heat and order-parameter curves in Fig. 10(a–c) and guides the eye through the 250-seed ensemble in Fig. 10(c).

It undergoes a first order transition at finite temperature which selects ground states consisting of AFM-ordered planes [176, 175] driven by an order-by-disorder mechanism [92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97].     q~=Q3​z2−r2+i​Qx2−y2=|q~|​ei​ϑ.\tilde{q}=Q_{3z^{2}-r^{2}}+iQ_{x^{2}-y^{2}}=|\tilde{q}|e^{i\vartheta}.

The six pure-uniaxial ±(3​c2−r2)\cramped{\pm(3c^{2}-r^{2})} order parameters correspond to ϑ∈(2​π/6)​ℤ\cramped{\vartheta\in(2\pi/6)\mathbbm{Z}}, while the six pure-biaxial ±(a2−b2)\cramped{\pm(a^{2}-b^{2})} order parameters with Tr⁡[Q3]=0\cramped{\Tr[Q^{3}]=0} correspond to ϑ∈(2​π/6)​(ℤ+1/2)\cramped{\vartheta\in(2\pi/6)(\mathbbm{Z}+1/2)}. This free energy is then formally equivalent to that describing the development of so-called “ψ2\psi_{2}” (uniaxial) and “ψ3\psi_{3}” (biaxial) orders in anisotropic pyrochlore spin models, in which biaxial states are selected by a (dangerously) irrelevant sixth-order cos⁡(6​ϑ)\cos(6\vartheta) term [123, 36, 3, 16]. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
